# Components reference

Generated from the engine's reflection data. Version marks: a component added after 0.1.0 has a "Since 0.1.x." line under its heading, and a field added later than its component ends with "(since 0.1.x)"; "Not released yet" means it is only on the main branch, in no download. Nothing is printed for what existed in 0.1.0; if your factoria is older than a mark, that item is missing there. The scripting API at the end marks its functions, types and members the same way, with a JSDoc `@since` tag. In scene JSON a component is `"Name": { field: value, ... }` (omitted fields keep their defaults); in scripts use `entity.get("Name")`. Vectors accept `[x, y]` or `{x, y}`; colors accept `[r, g, b, a]` (0..1) or `"#rrggbb"`.

## Core

### EntityInfo

Identity of an entity; present on every entity. In scene files these fields are the entity's top-level keys (id, name, tags, active), not a component entry. Tags are handled by the scene serializer.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | `""` | Stable unique string id within the scene (e.g. "player"). Used to reference the entity from Entity fields, scripts (world.find) and tools. Auto-generated ("e1", "e2"...) if omitted. |
| `name` | string | `""` | Display name shown in the editor and logs. Not unique. |
| `active` | bool | `true` | If false the entity and all its children are skipped by rendering, physics, audio and scripts. |

### Transform

Position, rotation and scale of an entity relative to its parent. Present on every entity. 2D uses x/y of position and the z angle of rotation; 3D units are meters.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `position` | vec3 | `[0.0,0.0,0.0]` | Local position relative to the parent [x, y, z]. 2D: x right, y up, z is only used for depth ordering of 3D content. Units: world units (design pixels in 2D, meters in 3D). |
| `rotation` | vec3 | `[0.0,0.0,0.0]` | Local rotation as euler angles in DEGREES [pitch around X, yaw around Y, roll around Z], applied in the order Y, X, Z. 2D games only use the z value (counter-clockwise). |
| `scale` | vec3 | `[1.0,1.0,1.0]` | Local scale [x, y, z]. 1 = original size; negative values mirror. |

## Camera

### Camera

Renders the scene to the screen. Every active camera with primary=true draws its view into its viewport (the whole screen by default), in ascending depth order: the lowest depth draws first and is "the" camera (camera.main; the bloom and colorFilter of the frame are its). Two or more cameras with their own viewport make split-screen (two players side by side, four in quarters) or an inset (a minimap). Each camera culls, lights and sorts its own view; screen-space items (UI, HUD) are drawn once over the whole screen, after all the cameras. 3D cameras look down their local -Z axis.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `projection` | enum: orthographic \\| perspective | `"orthographic"` | orthographic: flat 2D view (no perspective). perspective: 3D view with depth. |
| `fov` | float | `60.0` | Perspective only: vertical field of view in degrees. Range 1.0..179.0. |
| `orthoSize` | float | `0.0` | Orthographic only: half of the visible height in world units. 0 = use the design resolution (pixel perfect: one world unit is one design pixel). Range 0.0..100000.0. |
| `nearPlane` | float | `0.1` | Perspective only: distance of the near clip plane in meters. Keep it as large as possible for depth precision. Range 0.001..100000.0. |
| `farPlane` | float | `1000.0` | Perspective only: distance of the far clip plane in meters. Range 0.01..1000000.0. |
| `clearColor` | color | `[0.08,0.08,0.12,1.0]` | Background color the camera clears to when clear is true. |
| `clear` | bool | `true` | Clear this camera's viewport to clearColor before it draws. Set false on an overlay camera that draws on top of what an earlier camera (a lower depth) drew in the same area. The first camera in depth order clears the whole target, also the part its viewport does not cover; a camera with clear false first in depth order keeps the previous frame under it. |
| `primary` | bool | `true` | true: this camera renders (when it is active), into its viewport, in depth order with the other primary cameras. false: it does not render (an unused camera, or one a script switches on for a split screen). |
| `depth` | int | `0` | Draw order of the cameras: the lowest depth draws first, the highest on top where viewports overlap. The lowest is the camera that camera.main, a screen conversion without a camera and the post effects (bloom, colorFilter) use. Cameras with the same depth keep the order of creation. |
| `viewport` | rect | `[0.0,0.0,1.0,1.0]` | The part of the screen this camera draws into: [x, y, width, height], each from 0 to 1, with [0, 0] the TOP-LEFT corner and +Y down (like screen space). The fractions count the GAME TARGET (what `viewportSpace` says): not the pixels of the window, whose letterbox bars (a window with another shape than the game) are outside it. [0, 0, 1, 1] (default) is the whole screen, [0, 0, 0.5, 1] the left half, [0.5, 0, 0.5, 1] the right half, [0, 0, 0.5, 0.5] the top-left quarter, [0.7, 0.05, 0.25, 0.25] a minimap inset. x + width and y + height must not pass 1 and the size must be above 0, or the scene fails to load. The aspect ratio follows the rectangle: an orthographic camera with orthoSize 0 keeps one world unit per design pixel (it sees half the width in a half-width viewport); with an orthoSize it keeps the same visible height, so set it equal on the cameras of a split screen to give every player the same zoom. Each camera is culled and lit on its own, so a Light2D only lights the cameras it reaches. The post effects (bloom, colorFilter, bloomScreenSpace) are applied once to the finished frame with the settings of the lowest-depth camera; the other cameras' values are ignored. UI and screen-space items cover the whole screen, not one viewport. camera.screenToWorld(point, camera) and camera.at(point) tell which camera is under a screen point. To show a camera INSIDE a widget of the UI instead (an item on a stage in a menu, a map in a panel) give it a CameraView: that fits the rectangle of the widget, with the clipping, layering and mirroring of the UI, and ignores this field. (since 0.3.0) |
| `viewportSpace` | enum: screen \\| design | `"screen"` | Which rectangle the fractions of `viewport` count. screen (default): the whole game target, that is the design resolution, or the area the Expand scale mode grows it to for a window with another shape (the letterbox bars of the Fit modes are not part of it). design: the design resolution (display.designWidth x designHeight) from the top-left corner, which is where a UI laid out from anchor [0, 0] in design pixels sits, so a viewport of [430 / 1280, 84 / 720, 400 / 1280, 360 / 720] lands on the same pixels as a 400 x 360 Panel at [430, 84] even when Expand has grown the target. The two are the same in every mode but Expand. For a rectangle that follows a widget, use a CameraView. (since 0.3.0) |
| `lighting` | enum: scene \\| studio | `"scene"` | What lights the 3D meshes this camera draws. scene (default): the Light entities, SceneSettings.ambientLight, the sky and environment colours and the fog of the scene. studio: a rig that follows the camera instead, whatever the scene holds and wherever the camera is: a warm key light from the upper left, a cool fill from the right, a rim light from behind, a neutral ambient and environment for reflections, no sky (the camera paints clearColor), no fog, no shadows. Scene lights do not reach the camera and a 2D lit sprite it draws is lit by the ambient alone (full brightness). Use it for an item turning on a stage in a menu (CameraView), or a portrait, that must look the same in a dark cellar and in a bright field. MeshRenderer.unlit meshes are not affected. Scale the rig with studioIntensity. (since 0.3.0) |
| `studioIntensity` | float | `1.0` | Only used when lighting is studio. Multiplies the brightness of the studio rig (the three lights, the ambient and the environment): 1 (default) shows a mid-grey surface at about its own colour, 0.5 is dimmer, 2 is bright and may wash out pale colours. Range 0.0..8.0. (since 0.3.0) |
| `bloom` | bool | `false` | Bloom (glow) post-process: bright pixels bleed light into their surroundings, the neon / laser / fire / explosion look. Works for 2D and 3D cameras, is applied to the whole finished frame (screen-space HUD included, unless bloomScreenSpace is false) and shows in screenshots. Combine with blend "additive" on Sprite, Shape2D or ParticleEmitter instead of hand-drawing blurred halo sprites. Off by default; costs a few extra render passes per frame (cheap on a GPU, about 5 ms at 1280x720 on the software renderer used for headless runs). Tune with bloomThreshold, bloomIntensity and bloomRadius; keep the HUD crisp with bloomScreenSpace. With several cameras the bloom settings of the lowest-depth camera apply to the whole frame. |
| `bloomThreshold` | float | `0.7` | Only used when bloom is true. Brightness (0..1, the largest of a pixel's r, g, b) at which glow starts: pixels at or below it do not glow, the glow ramps up linearly to full strength at 1 (white / fully saturated). Lower it (0.3-0.6) to make dim colors glow too; raise it (0.9+) so only the brightest pixels do (values above 0.99 behave like 0.99). Range 0.0..1.0. |
| `bloomIntensity` | float | `1.2` | Only used when bloom is true. Strength of the glow that is added back onto the frame: 0 = none, 1 = the blurred bright pixels are added once, 2 = twice (brighter, saturates sooner). Limited to 0..10. Range 0.0..10.0. |
| `bloomRadius` | float | `20.0` | Only used when bloom is true. How far the glow reaches, in design pixels (1280x720 by default): a gaussian blur whose visible halo fades out roughly this far from the bright pixels. Values below ~5 behave like 5 (the glow is computed at reduced resolution, and larger radii at even lower resolution, so wide glows are softer). Limited to 1..128. Range 1.0..128.0. |
| `bloomScreenSpace` | bool | `true` | Only used when bloom is true. true (default): the whole finished frame glows, screen-space items (Sprite, Shape2D, Text with space "screen", and debug text) included, so a bright neon title or HUD icon glows too. false: screen-space items are drawn AFTER the bloom, so the HUD (score, lives, menus) stays crisp and never glows while the world still does. Set it to false whenever the HUD has white or bright text over a glowing world; leave it true to make a screen-space title or logo glow. |
| `colorFilter` | enum: none \\| greyscale \\| highContrast \\| protanopia \\| deuteranopia \\| tritanopia | `"none"` | Accessibility colour filter, the LAST post-process pass: it is applied to the whole finished frame (HUD included, after the bloom) on every graphics backend, so screenshots, factoria run --screenshot-at and --record-video show it too. A game's options screen sets it from the player's choice (it is not saved by itself). none (default): no pass, no cost. greyscale: Rec. 709 luminance in linear light. highContrast: contrast stretched 1.8x around mid grey, clipped. protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia: a daltonize correction for a player who lacks that cone: the loss is estimated with the Machado 2009 matrix (severity 1.0) and the lost information is shifted into the channels the player still sees (Fidaner's method), so colours that collapse together (red vs green) differ in brightness or in the remaining hue. To CHECK a game without changing what the player sees, use the `simulate` option of game.screenshot / --screenshot-simulate instead. With several cameras the lowest-depth camera's filter covers the whole frame. (since 0.2.0) |
| `renderTarget` | string | `""` | Makes this camera draw into a TEXTURE instead of the screen, live every frame: a name such as "book". The texture is the id "target:book" and goes wherever a texture path does: MeshRenderer.texture or normalMap (a screen on a 3D model, a page of a book, a mirror), a texture parameter of a material (materialParams), Sprite.texture, Panel.texture, Button.icon. A camera with a name draws only into its texture: it is not drawn to the screen, ignores viewport, primary and clear (it always clears to clearColor, alpha included, so a transparent target composes over what is behind it) and is never camera.main nor the audio listener. It still has to be active (entity and ancestors). The target is drawn BEFORE the cameras that show it in the same frame, so there is no lag; a camera whose own view shows its target gets a missing-texture checker there and one error that says so (a render loop needs two targets: A shows B and B shows A, each one frame late). The camera draws everything in its frustum unless you give it showTags / hideTags: tag what a target shows (the root of a 2D page of Text, Sprites, Buttons as world-space entities, tag "page_left"), give the target camera showTags ["page_left"] and the camera that draws the model hideTags ["page_left"], so each sees only its own content wherever it is in the world. Screen-space UI (Panel, Button and the other widgets, space "screen" items) is not drawn into a target: use world-space Sprite, Text and Shape2D, whose Interactable components still get the pointer through the mesh (docs/RENDERING.md, "Render targets"). Names are unique: a second camera with the same name is not drawn, with an error. "" (default) = the screen. Letters, digits, '_', '-' and '.', up to 64 characters. (since 0.9.0) |
| `renderTargetSize` | vec2 | `[1024.0,1024.0]` | Only used with renderTarget: the size of the texture in pixels, [width, height], each 1..4096 (default [1024, 1024]). The camera's aspect is this rectangle's, so an orthographic camera with orthoSize 0 sees one world unit per texture pixel and with an orthoSize it sees that half-height whatever the size. Changing it live remakes the texture; memory is about width x height x 8 bytes (4 more per pixel with antialiasing). (since 0.9.0) |
| `showTags` | json | `[]` | Culling mask, the allow list: an array of tag names (EntityInfo "tags"), default [] = no restriction. When it is not empty the camera draws only the entities that have one of these tags OR have an ancestor that does, so tagging the root of a page covers its Sprites, Text, Shape2D and every other child. Applies to what the camera draws in world space, on a screen camera and on one with renderTarget alike: Sprite, Shape2D, Text, Tilemap, ParticleEmitter and MeshRenderer (a world-space item; screen-space UI and items with space "screen" belong to the screen and ignore it). Lights are not filtered: a Light still lights everything its camera draws. An entity the camera does not draw casts no shadow in that camera's view, takes no click through it and is not picked by it: the pointer, Interactable hit tests (also through a mesh that shows a render target) and game.click only reach what the camera draws. Combine with hideTags: an entity is drawn when it passes showTags AND is not in hideTags. `factoria validate` warns about a tag no entity carries (with a did-you-mean) and rejects a tag in both lists. Example: the camera of a page, showTags ["page_left"]. Assign a whole new array to change it from a script (cam.showTags = ["page_right"]); a tag added with entity.addTag(...) takes effect on the next frame drawn. (since 0.12.0) |
| `hideTags` | json | `[]` | Culling mask, the block list: an array of tag names (EntityInfo "tags"), default [] = nothing hidden. The camera does not draw the entities that have one of these tags or have an ancestor that does, whatever showTags says; it applies to the same things (world-space Sprite, Shape2D, Text, Tilemap, ParticleEmitter, MeshRenderer; shadows, pointer and game.click follow) and spares screen-space UI. Use it on the camera that draws a 3D model with render-target pages so it does not also see the pages' own content: hideTags ["page_left", "page_right"]. A tag in both showTags and hideTags is an error for `factoria validate`. (since 0.12.0) |

## 2D

### Sprite

Draws a textured (or solid color) quad. Use `region` to pick a frame from a sprite sheet. Draw order: higher `layer` on top; ties sort by position.y (lower y on top), then creation order.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `texture` | asset (texture) | `""` | Project-relative path of the image (e.g. "assets/hero.png"). Empty draws a solid quad of `color`. A picture made at run time (`render.captureTexture`, `render.textureFromPNG`) works here too: use its `id` ("runtime:3"; docs/SCRIPTING.md, "Render"). So does the live picture of a camera: "target:<name>" for the Camera whose `renderTarget` is that name (docs/RENDERING.md, "Render targets"). |
| `region` | rect | `[0.0,0.0,0.0,0.0]` | Source rectangle [x, y, w, h] in texture pixels with the origin at the TOP-LEFT. A zero size means the whole texture. SpriteAnimator overwrites it every frame. |
| `size` | vec2 | `[0.0,0.0]` | Size [w, h] in world units. [0, 0] = use the region (or texture) size in pixels. |
| `pivot` | vec2 | `[0.5,0.5]` | Anchor inside the sprite: [0, 0] bottom-left, [0.5, 0.5] center, [1, 1] top-right. |
| `color` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]` | Tint multiplied with the texture. Alpha makes it translucent. Accepts [r,g,b,a], "#rrggbb" or a name. |
| `flipX` | bool | `false` | Mirror horizontally. |
| `flipY` | bool | `false` | Mirror vertically. |
| `layer` | int | `0` | Draw order. Higher layers draw on top of lower ones. Backgrounds use negative layers. |
| `space` | enum: world \\| screen | `"world"` | world: positioned in the game world and affected by cameras. screen: UI/HUD in design-resolution pixels with (0,0) at the TOP-LEFT and +Y DOWN; drawn after the world. |
| `pixelArt` | bool | `true` | true = nearest-neighbour filtering (crisp pixels), false = smooth linear filtering. |
| `blend` | enum: alpha \\| additive \\| multiply | `"alpha"` | Compositing: alpha (normal), additive (glow, neon, fire, lasers; brightens), multiply (darkens/tints). |
| `anchor` | vec2 | `[0.0,0.0]` | Screen space only: screen point the position is relative to. [0,0] top-left (default), [1,0] top-right, [0.5,0.5] center, [1,1] bottom-right. Keeps HUD elements glued to screen edges on any aspect ratio. |
| `safeArea` | bool | `false` | Screen space only. true: the anchor names a point of the SAFE area, the screen minus the notch, rounded corners and system bars of a phone (screen.safeArea in scripts), instead of the whole screen: anchor [0, 0] is the top-left corner of the safe area, [1, 1] its bottom-right. Keeps HUD and buttons out of the notch. On a screen without cutouts (desktop, most tablets) it changes nothing. Default false. (since 0.2.0) |
| `slice` | vec4 | `[0.0,0.0,0.0,0.0]` | 9-slice borders in texture pixels [left, top, right, bottom], measured inside `region` (or the whole texture). With a border set the four corners are drawn at their texture size (1 texture pixel = 1 world unit), the edges stretch along one axis and the centre along both, so one small frame gives a panel, bar or platform of any `size`. [0, 0, 0, 0] (default) stretches the whole region. Borders that do not fit in `size` shrink together. Works with atlas-packed textures, flipX / flipY and a lit sprite. Screen-space UI panels use the same slicing through Panel.texture and Panel.slice. (since 0.2.0) |
| `lit` | bool | `false` | World space only. true: the sprite is shaded by the Light2D entities of the scene plus SceneSettings.ambientLight (its colour is multiplied by ambient + the sum of the lights); false (default): drawn exactly as the texture says, whatever lights exist. How many lights shade a frame: see Light2D. (since 0.2.0) |
| `normalMap` | asset (texture) | `""` | Lit sprites only. Tangent-space normal map: RGB = (x, y, z) mapped from 0..1 to -1..1, +x to the right and +y UP the picture (OpenGL / Unity convention), laid out exactly like `texture` and `region` (same size). It turns with the sprite's rotation and flips. Empty (default) = a flat sprite lit only by distance. Ignored unless `lit` is true. (since 0.2.0) |
| `skew` | vec2 | `[0.0,0.0]` | Shear in degrees [x, y] about the pivot, applied before the entity's rotation and scale: x = 20 leans the top edge to the right (an italic slant, a sign swinging in wind, a page seen at an angle), x = -20 to the left; y = 20 tilts the right edge up (a flag in a gust). Each angle is clamped to -80..80. [0, 0] (default) = no shear. Works with a deformable sprite (the shear is applied after the vertex offsets), a lit sprite and a screen-space sprite; it also shears the picking box of the editor and the entity's bounds. (since 0.4.0) |
| `meshColumns` | int | `0` | Makes the sprite deformable: it is drawn as a grid of meshColumns x meshRows cells (so (meshColumns + 1) x (meshRows + 1) vertices) that textures `region` evenly, and `vertexOffsets` moves the vertices. Needs meshRows > 0 too. 0 (default) = a plain quad. A side above 128 is clamped to 128; a grid of more than 4096 cells (columns x rows) is drawn as a plain quad and a warning is logged once per scene. A bent page, a flag or cloth is ONE entity with e.g. 16 columns x 1 row or 8 x 8. A deformable sprite ignores `slice` (9-slice). It costs one quad per cell, still in the sprite's batch: draw calls do not grow. Range 0.0..128.0. (since 0.4.0) |
| `meshRows` | int | `0` | Grid cells down for a deformable sprite (see meshColumns). 0 (default) = a plain quad. Range 0.0..128.0. (since 0.4.0) |
| `vertexOffsets` | json | `[]` | Deformable sprites only (meshColumns > 0 and meshRows > 0): how far each grid vertex is moved from its place, in the sprite's local units (the size it is drawn at, before scale and rotation; +x right, +y UP). A flat array of numbers [dx0, dy0, dx1, dy1, ...] with an x and a y per vertex, row by row starting at the TOP row and going left to right: vertex (column c, row r) is at index (r * (meshColumns + 1) + c) * 2. A shorter array leaves the vertices it does not name in place; extra numbers are ignored; a value that is not a number counts as 0. Write the whole array to change it (a script sets it every frame: `e.get('Sprite').vertexOffsets = offsets`; changing one element of the array it returned does not write back). The texture is stretched with the vertices, so offsets bend the picture. [] (default) = the undeformed grid. Offsets do not change `size`, but the bounds of the entity (entity.bounds(), editor picking) cover the moved vertices. (since 0.4.0) |
| `vertexColors` | json | `[]` | Deformable sprites only (meshColumns > 0 and meshRows > 0): a colour for every grid vertex, multiplied with `color` (and Tint), blended smoothly across each cell. A flat array of numbers [r0, g0, b0, a0, r1, g1, b1, a1, ...], components 0..1, one RGBA per vertex in the order of `vertexOffsets` (row by row from the TOP row, left to right): vertex (column c, row r) starts at index (r * (meshColumns + 1) + c) * 4. The length must be exactly (meshColumns + 1) * (meshRows + 1) * 4: a scene or prefab with another length is an error naming the length it needs, and a script that writes a wrong length gets one warning and the colours are ignored. A bent page gets its light and dark along the curve with [0.6,0.6,0.6,1] at the vertices in shade and [1,1,1,1] in light. Write the whole array to change it (like vertexOffsets). [] (default) = every vertex white. Not used with SpriteSkin. (since 0.9.0) |

### Tint

Since 0.4.0.

Multiplies a colour (and an opacity) into every 2D visual of this entity and of all its children, grandchildren and so on: Sprite, Shape2D, Text (glyph colours and rich-text colours too), Tilemap, ParticleEmitter, and the screen-space UI widgets (Panel, Button, Toggle, Slider, TextField, ScrollList, the touch controls, Video, CameraView, Chart, Captions) drawn by the renderer. Put it on the root of a group to fade it out (color [1, 1, 1, 0.5]), turn it red (a damage flash), or darken a whole room, without touching each visual. The tints of an entity and all its ancestors multiply together, so nested groups compose; alpha is multiplied too (a 0.5 inside a 0.5 shows at 0.25), and a visual whose resulting opacity is 0 is not drawn. It multiplies the colours the visual already has (Sprite.color, Shape2D.color and color2 and every gradient stop, Text.color, Tilemap.color, a particle's own colour over its life, Panel.color) and does not affect 3D MeshRenderer, lights, the debug draw or the camera. Entities without a Tint ancestor cost nothing extra: the renderer only walks the parents when at least one Tint exists in the scene.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `color` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]` | RGBA multiplied into the colour of the visuals of this entity and its descendants. [1, 1, 1, 1] (default) changes nothing. Alpha is a group opacity: [1, 1, 1, 0.5] draws the group at half opacity (each visual is faded on its own, so overlapping visuals of the group still show through one another). Accepts [r,g,b,a], "#rrggbb" or a name. |

### Parallax

Since 0.2.0.

Shifts the drawing of this entity's world-space visuals (Sprite, Shape2D, Text, Tilemap) with the camera so far layers slide slower than near ones. Offset = camera position * (1 - factor) per axis: factor 1 behaves like any world object, 0 stays glued to the camera (a sky), 0.5 is half as fast (distant hills), above 1 is a foreground. With the camera at (0, 0) the entity is exactly where its Transform says. Only the drawing moves: Transform, physics and picking positions stay put, while entity.bounds() reports where it is drawn. Deterministic: it depends only on the camera position.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `factor` | vec2 | `[0.5,0.5]` | [x, y] fraction of the camera's movement this layer follows (0 = fixed on screen, 1 = a normal world object). |
| `repeatX` | bool | `false` | Sprite only. Tile the sprite endlessly left and right (at `repeatSize.x` spacing, or its own width) so a background strip never runs out. The copies are drawn only where the camera sees them. |
| `repeatY` | bool | `false` | Sprite only. Same as repeatX, up and down. |
| `repeatSize` | vec2 | `[0.0,0.0]` | Distance between repeated copies in world units [x, y]. 0 = the sprite's own width / height. Use a smaller value to overlap soft edges, a larger one for gaps. |
| `offset` | vec2 | `[0.0,0.0]` | Runtime: the shift [x, y] currently applied to the drawing (written by the renderer every frame). Read-only. Runtime-only (not saved). |

### Light2D

Since 0.2.0.

A light for lit 2D visuals: sprites, shapes and tilemaps with `lit` true. Their colour is multiplied by SceneSettings.ambientLight plus the light of every Light2D (point: color * intensity * (1 - distance / radius)^falloff, scaled by the normal map's angle to the light when the sprite has a normalMap; directional: even light from one direction). Unlit visuals ignore lights, so existing games look the same. Point lights are added up in a light buffer the size of the picture (SceneSettings.lightScale), so a scene can have hundreds: at most 256 lights shade a frame, directional lights first, then the point lights whose radius reaches the camera view (the ones with more of their radius in view first, then the more intense ones); a light entirely off-view is left out. More than 256 in view logs one warning per scene, and renderStats().lights2d / lights2dDropped count what was kept and left out. A lit sprite or tile WITH a normal map is shaded per pixel by the first 16 of those lights (directional first), the rest only lights flat surfaces. `castShadows` lets the solid tiles of a Tilemap with occludesLight cast shadows (at most 32 shadow-casting lights per frame). The light sits at the entity's position (Transform) and ignores layers.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `type` | enum: point \\| directional | `"point"` | point: a lamp at the entity's position that fades out at `radius`. directional: sun / moon, the same everywhere, coming from the opposite of `direction`. |
| `color` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]` | Light colour. Accepts [r,g,b,a], "#rrggbb" or a name (alpha is ignored). |
| `intensity` | float | `1.0` | Strength: multiplies color. 1 = full colour at the lamp; above 1 over-brightens. Range 0.0..100.0. |
| `radius` | float | `300.0` | Point lights: distance in world units at which the light has faded to nothing. Range 0.0..100000.0. |
| `falloff` | float | `2.0` | Point lights: fade curve exponent. 1 = linear, 2 (default) = smooth, higher = a tight bright core. Range 0.01..16.0. |
| `height` | float | `80.0` | Point lights: height above the drawing plane in world units. Only matters for normal-mapped sprites: a low lamp grazes the surface and shows relief, a high one lights it flatly. Range 0.0..100000.0. |
| `direction` | float | `270.0` | Directional lights: degrees the light travels towards (0 = right, 90 = up, 270 = down). |
| `elevation` | float | `45.0` | Directional lights: angle above the drawing plane in degrees (90 = straight at the picture, 0 = along it). Range 0.0..90.0. |
| `castShadows` | bool | `false` | Point lights: true = the solid tiles of every Tilemap with occludesLight block this light, so the far side of a wall stays dark. The first solid tile the light reaches is lit (its face); the tiles and floor behind it are in shadow. A light placed inside a solid tile shines out of it. Shadows follow tile edits (set_tile) on the next frame. Costs more than a plain light: see PERFORMANCE.md; at most 32 shadow-casting lights are shaded per frame (the ones ranked first), the others shine through walls. Directional lights cast no shadows. Default false. (since 0.3.0) |

### SpriteAnimator

Flipbook animation over a grid sprite sheet. Requires a Sprite on the same entity; it overwrites Sprite.region every frame. Frames are numbered row-major from the top-left. Set `clip` to play a named clip of the texture's `sheet` entry in assets.json (grid, frames, fps, loop and pivot come from there; `assets.animate_svg`, `assets.bake_sheet`, `assets.slice_sheet` and the Aseprite import write it): a scene then names only the texture and the clip. The numeric fields override the clip when they differ from their default (columns 1, rows 1, firstFrame 0, lastFrame 0, fps 10, loop true). From a script: entity.spriteAnimator.play(name). A non-looping clip that reaches its end sends the game event `clipEnded` {id, clip}.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `columns` | int | `1` | Number of columns in the sprite sheet grid. With `clip`, set it (not 1) only to override the sheet entry. Range 1.0..4096.0. |
| `rows` | int | `1` | Number of rows in the sprite sheet grid. Range 1.0..4096.0. |
| `firstFrame` | int | `0` | First frame of the clip (inclusive, row-major index). |
| `lastFrame` | int | `0` | Last frame of the clip (inclusive, row-major index). |
| `fps` | float | `10.0` | Playback speed in frames per second. Range 0.0..1000.0. |
| `loop` | bool | `true` | Restart from firstFrame after lastFrame. If false the animation stops on the last frame and sends `clipEnded`. With `clip`, false overrides a looping clip; true (the default) leaves the clip's own loop. |
| `playing` | bool | `true` | Set false to pause, true to play. |
| `clip` | string | `""` | Name of a clip of the Sprite texture's `sheet` entry in assets.json ("run"); "" = none, the numeric fields alone. Changing it restarts the animation. A name the sheet does not have is an error that lists the clips ("did you mean"): `factoria validate` finds it in scenes, a script's play(name) throws it, a running game logs it once and shows the first frame. (since 0.6.0) |
| `mode` | enum: forward \\| reverse \\| pingpong | `"forward"` | Order of the frames: forward (first to last), reverse (last to first) or pingpong (first to last and back, without repeating the end frames). A pingpong clip that does not loop stops back on the first frame. (since 0.6.0) |
| `sheetPivot` | bool | `true` | true = the pivot recorded in the sheet entry (or the clip's own pivot) is used as Sprite.pivot while the Sprite's own pivot is the default centre [0.5, 0.5]; a Sprite that sets another pivot keeps it. The sheet stores it from the TOP-left of the frame, Sprite.pivot counts from the bottom-left, so y is flipped. false = never touch the pivot. (since 0.6.0) |
| `ended` | bool | `false` | Runtime state: a non-looping clip reached its end (clipEnded was sent). Runtime-only (not saved). (since 0.6.0) |
| `playedClip` | string | `""` | Runtime state: the clip `time` counts in. Runtime-only (not saved). (since 0.6.0) |
| `time` | float | `0.0` | Runtime state: seconds elapsed in the current clip. Runtime-only (not saved). |
| `frame` | int | `0` | Runtime state: current frame index. Runtime-only (not saved). |

### Bone2D

Since 0.7.0.

A bone of a 2D skeleton, on a plain entity of the hierarchy (docs/ANIMATION.md, "Bones and IK"). The bone starts at the entity's origin and runs `length` units along its local +X axis, so its tip is where a child bone is usually put (position [length, 0]). Bones nest by being children of each other; a clip, a script or IK2D poses a bone through its Transform (rotation.z turns it, position and scale move and stretch it). A SpriteSkin deforms a Sprite's mesh with the bones; the editor draws the bones of the selection, and `debug.bones()` draws them in a game.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `length` | float | `32.0` | How far the bone runs along the entity's local +X axis, from its origin to its tip, in local units (the entity's Transform.scale stretches it). The tip is where the weights of a SpriteSkin and the IK2D solvers measure to. 32 by default. Range 0.0..100000.0. |
| `minAngle` | float | `-180.0` | The lowest Transform.rotation.z (degrees, in the parent's frame) IK2D may give this bone. Only IK2D keeps a bone inside the limits: a clip or a script can pose it anywhere. With maxAngle - minAngle of 360 or more (the default -180 .. 180) the bone is free. Example: a knee that only bends one way is minAngle 0, maxAngle 150. Range -360.0..360.0. |
| `maxAngle` | float | `180.0` | The highest Transform.rotation.z (degrees, in the parent's frame) IK2D may give this bone; see minAngle. Range -360.0..360.0. |

### SpriteSkin

Since 0.7.0.

Deforms the Sprite on the same entity with bones (docs/ANIMATION.md, "Bones and IK"): each vertex of the sprite's 2D mesh follows up to 4 bones, so one picture bends at an elbow or a tail without cutting it in pieces. The mesh is the Sprite's meshColumns x meshRows grid, or with `outline` a grid cut to the texture's opaque pixels. The skin remembers where the bones were when it was bound (`bindPose`: the first time the engine sees it, so pose the bones at rest in the scene; write `bindPose` as [] to bind again at the current pose). A bone that moves from its bind pose drags its vertices with it; at the bind pose the sprite looks exactly as without a skin. It is deformed on the CPU into the sprite's own batch: no extra draw call and no shader. World-space sprites only. Needs Sprite.meshColumns / meshRows or `outline`; Sprite.vertexOffsets still apply (before the bones) and Sprite.skew after them.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bones` | json | `[]` | The bones that move this sprite: an array of strings, each the id of a Bone2D entity ("hip") or the name of one, or a path of names ("skeleton/arm/hand"). A name or path is looked up under the sprite's entity, then under its parent, then under the grandparent and so on, so a character prefab can be instanced many times; an id is looked up in the whole scene. The order is the bone index of `weights` and `bindPose`. At most 64 bones. A name that finds no Bone2D is logged once, with a "did you mean", and that bone is left out. [] = no skin. |
| `weights` | json | `"auto"` | How the vertices follow the bones. "auto" (default): each vertex follows the nearest bones (at most 4), weighted by 1 / (distance to the bone's segment)^2 from the bind pose, so a vertex on a bone follows it alone and one between two joints blends them; it is the same every run. Or an array with one entry per grid vertex, in the order of Sprite.vertexOffsets (row by row from the TOP row, left to right; with `outline` the full grid, vertices the outline leaves out are skipped): an entry is [bone, weight, bone, weight, ...] with up to 4 pairs, `bone` an index into `bones`, weights normalised to 1; a missing or empty entry leaves the vertex where it is. |
| `bindPose` | json | `[]` | Where each bone was when the skin was bound, relative to the sprite: 6 numbers [a, b, c, d, tx, ty] per bone (the bone's 2D matrix in the sprite's local space). The engine writes it the first time it sees the skin; [] binds again, at the pose the bones have then. If its length does not match `bones` it is recorded again. |
| `outline` | bool | `false` | true: instead of Sprite.meshColumns / meshRows, the mesh is a grid of outlineDetail cells along the sprite's longer side, keeping only the cells that hold opaque pixels (alpha above 5%) of the texture's region, so a thin limb or a tail costs vertices where it is and transparent corners cost nothing. Needs the texture as an image file in the project (png, jpg, tga, bmp): a texture an export packed into an atlas, a `.ktx2` only or a picture made at run time draws the full grid instead, with one warning. Hot reload of the texture retraces it. |
| `outlineDetail` | int | `16` | outline only: how many cells the grid has along the sprite's longer side (the shorter side gets as many as keep the cells square). More cells follow the shape closer and deform smoother, at one quad per kept cell. 16 by default. Range 2.0..64.0. |

### IK2D

Since 0.7.0.

Inverse kinematics for a chain of Bone2D entities: put it on the LAST bone (the hand, the foot) and name a `target`; every fixed step, after the animators have posed the bones and before the frame is drawn, the bones from this one up through its parents are turned so the tip of this bone reaches the target entity's position, within each bone's minAngle / maxAngle. Feet on the ground, a hand on a lever, a head that looks at something (docs/ANIMATION.md, "Bones and IK"). The solvers are deterministic. A target out of reach leaves the chain straight, pointing at it. With several IK2D they solve in the order their components were added. IK2D rewrites the bones' rotation.z each step: the animator (or you) pose the bones before it, it adjusts them.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target` | entity |  | Id of the entity to reach: the tip of this bone (its origin plus Bone2D.length along its +X) is brought to the target's world position. Empty = the component does nothing. |
| `chainLength` | int | `2` | ccd: how many bones turn, this one and its parents upward (each must have a Bone2D and be the parent of the one before). twoBone ignores it: it always turns this bone and its parent. 2 by default. Range 1.0..16.0. |
| `bend` | enum: positive \\| negative | `"positive"` | twoBone: which way the middle joint (the elbow, the knee) bends. positive = this bone's rotation.z ends up counter-clockwise (greater) from the one above it, negative = clockwise. A character facing right with a knee in front usually wants one of them; flipping the whole character (a negative Transform.scale.x) is taken into account, so the knee stays in front. |
| `weight` | float | `1.0` | 0 to 1. 1 = the chain takes the solved pose; 0 = the animated pose stays; in between blends each bone's angle the short way round. Fade it in while a foot is planted, out in the air. Range 0.0..1.0. |
| `solver` | enum: twoBone \\| ccd | `"twoBone"` | twoBone: an exact solution for two bones (a leg, an arm), reaches whenever the target is within the two bones' length and honours `bend`. ccd: Cyclic Coordinate Descent, any chain of chainLength bones (a tail, a tentacle, a spine); it converges in at most 24 sweeps, bends where the limits allow and ignores `bend`. |

### Shape2D

Untextured 2D primitive for prototypes, UI panels and debug visuals.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `shape` | enum: rectangle \\| circle \\| line \\| triangle \\| diamond \\| polygon \\| star | `"rectangle"` | Kind of primitive to draw. triangle: isosceles, apex at the middle of the top edge of the size box, base along the bottom edge. diamond: a rhombus whose 4 points sit at the middles of the size box's 4 edges (a square rotated 45 degrees when size is square; handy for gems, enemies and neon markers). polygon: a regular polygon with `sides` sides whose vertices lie on the ellipse inscribed in the size box, first vertex pointing up (hexagons, pentagons, octagons; many sides approach a circle). star: `points` tips on that ellipse, first tip pointing up, with notches at `innerRadius` of the outer radius in between. Outlines (filled = false) of triangle, diamond, polygon and star grow INWARD from the silhouette, like the rectangle's, so a thick outline never pokes out of the size box. |
| `size` | vec2 | `[32.0,32.0]` | rectangle/triangle/diamond/polygon/star: [width, height] of the box that contains the shape. circle: diameter in x. line: end point offset from the entity origin. In screen space (space "screen", +Y down) a line's size.y points UP, unlike the size.y of Panels, Texts and Sprites, which grows downwards: size [100, 40] ends 100 px right and 40 px above the start, [100, -40] ends below it. A chart bar is a rectangle, not a line: give it pivot [0, 1] so size [w, h] hangs w right and h down from its position. |
| `color` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]` | Fill or outline color. |
| `filled` | bool | `true` | true = solid shape, false = outline only (lines are always drawn as strokes). |
| `thickness` | float | `2.0` | Outline / line thickness in world units. Range 0.0..10000.0. |
| `layer` | int | `0` | Draw order. Higher layers draw on top. |
| `space` | enum: world \\| screen | `"world"` | world: affected by cameras. screen: UI in design pixels, origin TOP-LEFT, +Y down. |
| `pivot` | vec2 | `[0.5,0.5]` | Anchor point within the shape's size box for every shape but line: [0.5,0.5] = the box centre sits on the position (default), [0,0] bottom-left, [1,1] top-right. This point is also what the entity rotates and scales around. In screen space +Y is down, so [0,1] puts the top-left corner at the position. For a triangle the box centre is NOT its centre of mass (the apex is at the top-middle, the base along the bottom): use [0.5, 0.3333] to put its centroid on the position, the natural point to spin a triangle around without it wobbling. Circles and diamonds are symmetric, so the default [0.5,0.5] already spins them in place. |
| `blend` | enum: alpha \\| additive \\| multiply | `"alpha"` | Compositing: alpha (normal), additive (glow/neon), multiply (darken). |
| `anchor` | vec2 | `[0.0,0.0]` | Screen space only: screen point the position is relative to ([0,0] top-left, [1,1] bottom-right). |
| `safeArea` | bool | `false` | Screen space only. true: the anchor names a point of the SAFE area, the screen minus the notch, rounded corners and system bars of a phone (screen.safeArea in scripts), instead of the whole screen: anchor [0, 0] is the top-left corner of the safe area, [1, 1] its bottom-right. Keeps HUD and buttons out of the notch. On a screen without cutouts (desktop, most tablets) it changes nothing. Default false. (since 0.2.0) |
| `sides` | int | `6` | polygon only: number of sides (3 = triangle, 6 = hexagon, 8 = octagon). Range 3.0..64.0. |
| `points` | int | `5` | star only: number of tips (5 = the classic star). Range 3.0..64.0. |
| `innerRadius` | float | `0.5` | star only: radius of the notches between the tips as a fraction of the outer radius. 0.5 = classic star, near 1 = a fat spiky polygon, near 0 = thin needles. Range 0.0..1.0. |
| `lit` | bool | `false` | World space only. true: the shape is shaded by the Light2D entities of the scene plus SceneSettings.ambientLight (its colour is multiplied by ambient + the sum of the lights), like Sprite.lit, so a dark level can use shapes for platforms and hazards; every shape type, outlines and lines included, is flat (no normal map). false (default): drawn exactly in `color`, whatever lights exist. How many lights shade a frame: see Light2D. (since 0.2.0) |
| `cornerRadius` | float | `0.0` | rectangle only: radius of the rounded corners in world units, antialiased (a button, a card, a page). Clamped to half the shorter side, so a large value makes a pill. 0 (default) = square corners, drawn as before. Other shapes ignore it. Range 0.0..100000.0. (since 0.4.0) |
| `softness` | float | `0.0` | rectangle and circle only: width in world units of a blurred edge, centred on the shape's outline (half of it fades in inside the outline, half outside, so the shape's footprint grows by softness / 2 on every side). Turns a shape into a soft drop shadow (a dark translucent rounded rectangle, a little offset, softness 12-30), a vignette or a light pool (a circle with softness near its diameter and an additive blend). Follows cornerRadius; works with filled = false (a blurred ring) and with a gradient. 0 (default) = a crisp, antialiased edge, as before. Triangles, diamonds, polygons, stars and lines ignore it (draw a circle or rectangle for a soft shape). Range 0.0..100000.0. (since 0.4.0) |
| `gradient` | enum: none \\| linear \\| radial | `"none"` | rectangle and circle fill only (filled = true): none (default) = flat `color`. linear = `color` blends to `color2` along the direction gradientAngle, from the box edge to the opposite edge (paper shading, a gutter, a sky). radial = `color` at the centre blends to `color2` at the edge of the shape's box (a vignette, a light pool, a glow); outside the box's inscribed ellipse it stays color2. The blend is computed per pixel (and dithered), so it is smooth with no banding, in one entity. Alpha is blended too (premultiplied, so a transparent color2 fades color out without greying it): make color2 transparent to fade out. A gradient whose `color` is transparent still draws when `color2` is not (the vignette); the shape is skipped only when every colour it uses is fully transparent. Ignored by outlines and by the other shapes. (since 0.4.0) |
| `color2` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]` | gradient only: the colour at the end of the gradient (the right/top end of a linear one, the edge of a radial one). `color` is the start. Include its alpha: [0, 0, 0, 0] fades `color` to nothing. (since 0.4.0) |
| `gradientAngle` | float | `0.0` | linear gradient only: direction in degrees, measured like a rotation (counter-clockwise, y up in world space): 0 = `color` on the left to `color2` on the right, 90 = `color` at the bottom to `color2` at the top, 270 = top to bottom. The gradient spans the shape's box exactly from corner to corner and turns with the entity. In screen space, where y is down, 90 still goes bottom to top on the screen. (since 0.4.0) |
| `gradientStops` | json | `[]` | gradient only: more than two colours. An array of [position, colour] pairs, position 0..1 along the gradient (0 = where `color` was, 1 = the far end or the edge of a radial one), colours as [r,g,b,a], "#rrggbb" or a name, e.g. [[0, "#000000cc"], [0.6, [0, 0, 0, 0.25]], [1, [0, 0, 0, 0]]] for a soft shadow that dies out slowly. Up to 8 stops (the others are ignored), sorted by position for you; before the first stop and after the last one the gradient keeps that stop's colour. Alpha blends like `color` -> `color2` (premultiplied). With stops, `color` and `color2` are not used for the fill, and the shape is skipped only when every stop is fully transparent. [] (default) = the two-colour gradient `color` -> `color2`. The colours are baked into a 256-step ramp (one row of a shared texture per distinct ramp, at most 256 ramps at once), so the cost is the same as a two-colour gradient, shapes with equal ramps still batch, and a script may change the stops every frame. An entry that is not [number, colour] is skipped with one warning. (since 0.4.0) |
| `gradientEase` | enum: linear \\| smoothstep \\| quadIn \\| quadOut \\| quadInOut \\| cubicIn \\| cubicOut \\| cubicInOut \\| quartIn \\| quartOut \\| quartInOut \\| quintIn \\| quintOut \\| quintInOut \\| sineIn \\| sineOut \\| sineInOut \\| expoIn \\| expoOut \\| expoInOut \\| circIn \\| circOut \\| circInOut | `"linear"` | gradient only: the curve the position follows before the colours are looked up, which removes the visible kink where a linear fade meets its end. The names are those of the script tween easings (docs/ANIMATION.md). linear (default) = even steps. A soft shadow or vignette that fades `color` -> a transparent `color2` looks natural with quadOut/cubicOut (fast start, long gentle tail, no edge) or smoothstep (no kink at either end); quadIn/cubicIn hold the start colour longer. It applies to the two-colour gradient and to gradientStops alike (stop positions are on the curve's input side: a stop at 0.5 is where the eased position is 0.5). The shape costs the same as a linear gradient. (since 0.4.0) |

### Text

Draws a string with a TrueType font (or the built-in font). Works in world and screen space.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `text` | string | `"Text"` | The string to draw. Use \n for line breaks. While `key` is set the engine overwrites it with the translation of the current language every frame: edit the string table (locales/<language>.json), not this field. |
| `key` | string | `""` | Localization key, e.g. "menu.play" (docs/LOCALIZATION.md). Empty (default) = this Text is not translated. With a key, the runtime writes the string of that key in the current language (locales/<language>.json, falling back to the base language and then to localization.defaultLanguage) into `text` when a scene or prefab loads, every frame and when the language changes, so `text` is overwritten at run time. A key that no string table has keeps the text written here and logs one warning. (since 0.2.0) |
| `keyArgs` | json | `{}` | Values for the {placeholders} of `key`, an object of name -> string or number: {"score": 12} fills "Score: {score}" (and `count` picks the form of a plural entry). Set it once from a script (`entity.set("Text", { keyArgs: { score } })` or `scene.set_component`) instead of rewriting the text every frame: the engine formats the translation with them when the text is localized, when the args change and when the language changes, so a language switch keeps them. Empty (default) = no arguments. Ignored while `key` is empty. (since 0.3.0) |
| `font` | asset (font) | `""` | Project-relative path of a .ttf font. Empty uses the built-in font, DejaVu Sans (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic). Other built-in fonts, by name: "builtin:pixel" (Press Start 2P, retro), "builtin:serif" (Crimson Text, a book serif with real bold, italic and bold italic), "builtin:hand" (Kalam, handwriting, with bold), "builtin:blackletter" (UnifrakturMaguntia, for titles) and "builtin:display" (IM Fell English, old print, with italic); the four after the pixel font have no Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew or Arabic (those fall back to DejaVu Sans) and an export ships just the ones a project names (docs/TEXT.md, "Built-in fonts"). Characters the font has no glyph for draw as nothing and log one warning per font: Chinese, Japanese and Korean need a .ttf that covers them (e.g. Noto Sans SC, JP or KR). Keep this empty and list the extra fonts in factoria.json (localization.fallbackFonts, localization.languageFonts) to cover every Text of the game (docs/TEXT.md). |
| `fontSize` | float | `24.0` | Glyph height in world units (pixels in 2D, meters in a 3D scene). A world Text may be tiny: 0.07 is 7 cm. The glyphs are rasterized for the size they have ON SCREEN, not for this number, so small world text stays sharp. Screen-space text is in design pixels (use 1 or more). docs/TEXT.md, "Text in a 3D scene". Range 0.001..4096.0. |
| `lit` | bool | `false` | World space only: true = the text is shaded by the scene's 3D lights (Light entities and SceneSettings.ambientLight) like a lit material, so gold lettering on a book cover darkens with the shading. The text is a flat surface facing its +Z (the side you read it from; seen from behind it uses the facing side); directional, point and spot lights are summed ONCE per Text, at the text's origin, and multiply `color` (and the colours and pictures of a rich text): no shadows, no per-pixel variation. false (default) = drawn unlit, exactly `color`. Ignored in screen space and under a Camera with lighting "studio". For a Text under 2D lights use a Sprite or Shape2D with `lit`. (since 0.9.0) |
| `color` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]` | Text color. |
| `align` | enum: left \\| center \\| right \\| start \\| end | `"left"` | Horizontal alignment of lines inside the text box. left / right are always the left / right edge, even for right-to-left text. start / end follow the current language: start = left and end = right in a left-to-right language, start = right and end = left in Arabic, Hebrew and the other right-to-left languages (i18n.direction), or when `direction` is rtl; use them for text that must read from its start side. |
| `pivot` | vec2 | `[0.0,1.0]` | Anchor of the text box: [0, 1] top-left (default), [0.5, 0.5] center, [1, 0] bottom-right. |
| `maxWidth` | float | `0.0` | If > 0, lines wrap at this width in world units. 0 = no wrapping. With autoShrink it is also the width the text must fit (a word longer than the box shrinks the font). Range 0.0..100000.0. |
| `maxHeight` | float | `0.0` | Box height in the same units as maxWidth that autoShrink fits the text into: a card title with maxWidth 200 and maxHeight 30 stays on one line at any text size by shrinking. 0 (default) = only the width counts. Nothing is clipped or wrapped by it; it only drives autoShrink and ui.overflowed(id). Range 0.0..100000.0. (since 0.3.0) |
| `autoShrink` | bool | `false` | true: when the text does not fit its box at the current text size (ui.textScale) and language, the font is made smaller until it does, never under `minFontSize` (so a German label in a fixed button stays inside at 200 % text, and a long translation is smaller instead of cut). It is decided every frame from the laid-out size, with no script. If it still does not fit at minFontSize it is drawn there and ui.overflowed(id) is true. false (default): the size is never reduced. (since 0.3.0) |
| `minFontSize` | float | `10.0` | autoShrink floor in design pixels, before ui.textScale (the floor is minFontSize times the player's text size, capped by maxTextScale, so the accessibility setting keeps working). Never above fontSize. Range 0.001..4096.0. (since 0.3.0) |
| `maxTextScale` | float | `0.0` | > 0: the player's text size (ui.textScale) stops growing this text at this scale, so a heading or a round button label does not outgrow its place: 1.3 means it is drawn at most 1.3 times its fontSize however big the option is. It only limits growth: at a text size below the cap it is drawn at the player's size. 0 (default) = no cap. Measuring (autoSize, layout, ui.measureText, ui.rectOf) and drawing use the same capped size. Range 0.0..3.0. (since 0.3.0) |
| `markup` | bool | `false` | true: the text reads tags: [b]bold[/b], [i]italic[/i] (the italic face of the font: factoria.json text.fonts "italic", or the built-in family's own, e.g. builtin:serif), [c:good]coloured[/c] (a name of factoria.json text.colors, a built-in colour name or #rrggbb) and [icon:fish] (a picture of text.icons, drawn inline as tall as the line); [[ is a literal [. Wrapping, alignment, maxWidth, autoShrink and ui.measureText all work on the visible characters, so the tags take no room. A tag the engine does not know is shown as written, `factoria validate` and ui.markupProblems(text) report it. false (default): the string is drawn as it is, so a [ in it is only a [. A run colour replaces the colour of the text and keeps its opacity. Docs: docs/TEXT.md, "Rich text". (since 0.3.0) |
| `bold` | bool | `false` | true: the whole text is bold. It uses the bold face the project gives the font (factoria.json text.fonts); a font with none is emboldened by the engine, and `factoria validate` suggests adding one. builtin:serif, builtin:hand and builtin:display bring real bold or italic faces of their own. [b] in markup does the same for a part of the text. false (default): regular weight. (since 0.3.0) |
| `direction` | enum: auto \\| ltr \\| rtl | `"auto"` | Base direction of the paragraphs (Unicode bidi). auto (default): the first strong letter decides, except that a Text with a localization key (`key`) takes the language's direction (i18n.direction), so a Hebrew line that starts with a key name or a {placeholder} filled with Latin text is still a right-to-left line, with no U+200F mark in the string. ltr / rtl: the paragraph runs that way whatever its first letter is. The direction also says which edge `align: start` is (rtl: the right one); the glyphs of a line keep their reading order whatever the alignment. Widget labels with a `key` follow the language the same way. (since 0.3.0) |
| `wordBreak` | enum: auto \\| normal \\| keepAll | `"auto"` | Where a wrapped line (maxWidth > 0) may end inside a run of letters with no space. auto (default): Korean keeps its words (Hangul lines end at spaces only, as Korean is written for screens), Chinese and Japanese break between any two characters (kinsoku keeps closing punctuation off the start of a line). normal: Hangul also breaks between syllables. keepAll: Hangul, Chinese and Japanese all break at spaces only; a run longer than maxWidth then overflows the box instead of splitting. No effect without maxWidth. (since 0.3.0) |
| `visibleCharacters` | int | `-1` | Typewriter reveal. -1 (default) draws the whole text. n >= 0 draws only its first n characters, counted in grapheme clusters (a letter with its accents, an emoji sequence or a Hangul syllable is one; spaces and line breaks count, the tags of `markup` do not and a [icon:name] picture is one). The text is laid out as a whole and only clipped, so the box, its wrapping, its alignment, ui.rectOf and a Panel that fits it keep the size of the full line while it reveals, and no word jumps to the next line. Reveal order is the order of the text, so a right-to-left line appears from its right end. Raise it from a script a few characters per second; a value above the length shows everything. Range -1.0..1000000.0. (since 0.3.0) |
| `layer` | int | `100` | Draw order. Higher layers draw on top. Text defaults above sprites. |
| `space` | enum: world \\| screen | `"world"` | world: affected by cameras. screen: HUD/UI in design pixels, origin TOP-LEFT, +Y down. |
| `anchor` | vec2 | `[0.0,0.0]` | Screen space only: screen point the position is relative to ([0,0] top-left, [1,0] top-right, [0.5,0] top-center, [1,1] bottom-right). Combine with pivot, e.g. anchor [1,0] + pivot [1,1] + position [-20, 20] = right-aligned 20px from the top-right corner. |
| `safeArea` | bool | `false` | Screen space only. true: the anchor names a point of the SAFE area, the screen minus the notch, rounded corners and system bars of a phone (screen.safeArea in scripts), instead of the whole screen: anchor [0, 0] is the top-left corner of the safe area, [1, 1] its bottom-right. Keeps HUD and buttons out of the notch. On a screen without cutouts (desktop, most tablets) it changes nothing. Default false. (since 0.2.0) |

### Tilemap

A grid of tiles drawn from a tileset texture; tile index -1 is empty. Row 0 is the TOP row. Solid tiles can generate static 2D collision.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tileset` | asset (texture) | `""` | Project-relative path of the tileset image (tiles laid out left-to-right, top-to-bottom). |
| `tileSize` | vec2 | `[16.0,16.0]` | Size of one tile [w, h], both in the tileset texture (pixels) and in the world (units). |
| `projection` | enum: orthogonal \\| isometric | `"orthogonal"` | How the cells lie in the world. "orthogonal" (default): square tiles of tileSize, tile (col, row) at x = col * tileSize.x, y = -row * tileSize.y from the entity's top-left corner. "isometric": diamond tiles, tileSize.x wide and groundHeight (default tileSize.y) high, 2:1 for the usual 100 x 50. +col runs down-right and +row down-left on screen; the entity's position is the TOP corner of the map (the top vertex of tile (0, 0)), tile (col, row) has its centre at ((col - row) * tileSize.x / 2, -(col + row + 1) * groundHeight / 2). The tiles are one batched mesh drawn row by row from row 0 and left to right, which is back to front, so a tile covers the edge of the ones behind it. Collision (a diamond per solid tile), light occluders, nav.findTilePath points and scene.import_ascii objects all follow it; entity.tilemap.cellAt / cellToWorld convert between cells and world points for both projections. (since 0.3.0) |
| `groundHeight` | float | `0.0` | Isometric only. Height of the ground diamond, in world units: the rows of the map are groundHeight / 2 apart. 0 (the default) = tileSize.y, a tile image that is exactly the diamond (tileSize [100, 50]). Set it when the tile image is taller than the diamond because it also shows the side of a block or a low wall: tileSize [100, 65] with groundHeight 50 is a 100 x 50 diamond with 15 units of side below it. Range 0.0..100000.0. (since 0.3.0) |
| `groundOffset` | float | `0.0` | Isometric only. How far the top corner of the ground diamond lies below the top edge of the tile image, in world units. 0 (the default) = the image starts at the diamond's top corner and anything taller hangs below it (a block side). Set it to the height of a tree or a wall that rises above the ground to draw the image that much higher: tileSize [100, 96], groundHeight 50, groundOffset 31 has 31 units above the diamond and 15 below. Range 0.0..100000.0. (since 0.3.0) |
| `columns` | int | `0` | Number of tile columns in the tileset texture (used to find a tile's source rectangle). Optional: 0 (the default) derives it from the tileset texture, as many whole tiles of tileSize.x as fit across its width. Set it only when the image has a different layout. Range 0.0..4096.0. |
| `margin` | int | `0` | Pixels between the edge of the tileset image and its first tile (the border many tileset packers add). Default 0: tiles start at the corner of the image. Used for the tile's source rectangle, for the tile count and for the normal map. Range 0.0..4096.0. (since 0.3.0) |
| `spacing` | int | `0` | Pixels between two neighbouring tiles of the tileset image (gutters, extruded borders). Default 0: tiles are packed edge to edge. With margin M and spacing S, tile (col, row) starts at (M + col*(tileSize.x+S), M + row*(tileSize.y+S)). Range 0.0..4096.0. (since 0.3.0) |
| `width` | int | `0` | Map width in tiles, for a flat tiles array. Not needed when tiles is an array of rows (the rows define the size; drawing and collision both use it). Range 0.0..65536.0. |
| `height` | int | `0` | Map height in tiles, for a flat tiles array. Not needed when tiles is an array of rows. Range 0.0..65536.0. |
| `tiles` | json | `[]` | Tile values, row-major with row 0 at the TOP: either a flat array of width*height integers (set width and height) or an array of rows (the size comes from the rows). -1 = empty. A value is the tileset index, optionally plus flags that mirror or turn that tile when drawn: 268435456 flips it left-right (flipX), 536870912 top-bottom (flipY), 1073741824 mirrors it across the diagonal (transpose). The image is transposed first, then flipped in x, then in y; a 90 degree clockwise turn is transpose + flipX = 1342177280 + index, 180 is flipX + flipY = 805306368 + index, 90 counter-clockwise is transpose + flipY = 1610612736 + index. scene.import_ascii legends write these for you: {"tile": 3, "rotate": 90, "flipX": true}. |
| `solidTiles` | json | `[]` | List of plain tile indices (no flip flags) that block movement; static colliders are generated for them. A flipped or rotated copy of a solid tile is still solid. Empty = nothing collides. |
| `terrains` | json | `[]` | Autotile rules: an array of terrains that tilemap.paint_terrain (scripts: entity.tilemap.paintTerrain) paints, choosing for every cell the edge, corner or inside tile that fits the cells around it. A terrain is {"name": "grass", "mode": "blob47", "first": 0}. mode: "basic16" looks at the 4 neighbours (16 tiles, slot = N*1 + E*2 + S*4 + W*8) and "blob47" at the 8 (47 tiles; a diagonal counts only when both cells next to it are in the terrain; the slots are the 47 reduced masks N=1 NE=2 E=4 SE=8 S=16 SW=32 W=64 NW=128 in ascending order, `factoria call image.tileset.info` prints them). The tiles come as "first": the tileset index of slot 0, the rest follow; or "tiles": one entry per slot, each a tile index or an array of tile indices that are variations of that look (one is picked from the cell's column, row and the terrain's "seed", the same every time). A cell belongs to the terrain whose tiles contain its tile index, so two terrains cannot share a tile. Optional: "seed" (integer, default 0), "joins" (names of terrains whose cells count as neighbours, e.g. a path that meets the grass), "outside": "terrain" (the map edge counts as this terrain, so no border is drawn there; default "empty"). image.tileset.build writes the terrain of a tileset it bakes; tilemap.set_terrains sets them from a rules file. Empty = no rules. (since 0.16.0) |
| `color` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]` | Tint multiplied with the tileset. |
| `layer` | int | `-10` | Draw order. Defaults below sprites (-10). |
| `lit` | bool | `false` | true: the tiles are shaded by the Light2D entities and SceneSettings.ambientLight, like Sprite.lit. Default false. (since 0.2.0) |
| `normalMap` | asset (texture) | `""` | Lit tilemaps only. Normal map image laid out exactly like the tileset (same size, same tile positions); flipped and rotated tiles turn their normals with them. Empty = flat tiles. (since 0.2.0) |
| `occludesLight` | bool | `false` | true: the tiles whose index is in solidTiles block the light of every Light2D with castShadows, so a wall hides what is behind it from the lamp (a cave, a dungeon, fog of war). The collision and the shadow use the same solidTiles. Editing a tile at run time (set_tile) moves the shadows on the next frame. The tilemap needs no `lit` itself to cast. Default false. (since 0.3.0) |

### ParticleEmitter

Emits short-lived particles (smoke, sparks, explosions). Particles interpolate size and color over their lifetime.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `emitting` | bool | `true` | Continuously emit while true. Set false to stop spawning (live particles finish). |
| `rate` | float | `20.0` | Particles emitted per second while emitting. Range 0.0..100000.0. |
| `burst` | int | `0` | Number of particles emitted once when the emitter starts (explosions). Range 0.0..100000.0. |
| `maxParticles` | int | `500` | Upper limit of simultaneously alive particles. Range 1.0..1000000.0. |
| `lifetime` | float | `1.0` | How long a particle lives, in seconds. Range 0.001..3600.0. |
| `lifetimeVariance` | float | `0.2` | Random +- fraction applied to lifetime (0.2 = +-20%). Range 0.0..1.0. |
| `speed` | float | `100.0` | Initial speed in world units per second. |
| `speedVariance` | float | `0.3` | Random +- fraction applied to speed. Range 0.0..1.0. |
| `direction` | float | `90.0` | 2D emission direction in degrees: 0 = right, 90 = up. |
| `spread` | float | `30.0` | Half-angle of the emission cone in degrees (180 = all directions). Range 0.0..180.0. |
| `gravity` | vec3 | `[0.0,-200.0,0.0]` | Constant acceleration [x, y, z] in world units/s^2 (default pulls down). |
| `startSize` | float | `8.0` | Particle size when born, in world units. |
| `endSize` | float | `0.0` | Particle size at the end of its life. |
| `startColor` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]` | Particle color when born. |
| `endColor` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,0.0]` | Particle color at the end of life (alpha 0 fades out). |
| `texture` | asset (texture) | `""` | Particle image. Empty uses a soft round particle. |
| `worldSpace` | bool | `true` | true = particles stay where they were emitted when the emitter moves; false = they follow the emitter. |
| `is3D` | bool | `false` | Emit in a 3D cone as camera-facing billboards instead of in the 2D plane. |
| `layer` | int | `50` | Draw order. Higher layers draw on top. |
| `blend` | enum: alpha \\| additive \\| multiply | `"alpha"` | Compositing of particles: additive is ideal for sparks, fire, magic and neon effects. |
| `autoDestroy` | bool | `false` | Destroy the entity automatically once it is not emitting and all its particles died. Use with burst > 0 and emitting = false for one-shot effects (explosions, pickups). |
| `space` | enum: world \\| screen | `"world"` | world: affected by cameras. screen: HUD/UI effects (menu sparks, score bursts) in design pixels, origin TOP-LEFT, +Y down, unaffected by cameras and drawn in the screen-space pass (so with Camera.bloomScreenSpace = false they are not bloomed). direction, gravity and speed keep their world meaning on screen: 90 = up, negative gravity y falls down the screen. Ignored (treated as world) when is3D is true. |
| `anchor` | vec2 | `[0.0,0.0]` | Screen space only: screen point the position is relative to ([0,0] top-left, [1,0] top-right, [0.5,0.5] center, [1,1] bottom-right). |
| `safeArea` | bool | `false` | Screen space only. true: the anchor names a point of the SAFE area, the screen minus the notch, rounded corners and system bars of a phone (screen.safeArea in scripts), instead of the whole screen: anchor [0, 0] is the top-left corner of the safe area, [1, 1] its bottom-right. Keeps HUD and buttons out of the notch. On a screen without cutouts (desktop, most tablets) it changes nothing. Default false. (since 0.2.0) |

## 3D

### MeshRenderer

Draws a 3D mesh with a PBR material (GGX highlights, sky reflections, normal maps; glTF materials are read). Needs a perspective Camera and (unless unlit) a Light to be visible.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mesh` | string | `"cube"` | Built-in shape name ("cube", "sphere", "plane", "cylinder", "capsule", "cone", "quad") or a project-relative path to a .gltf/.glb model (e.g. "assets/models/ship.glb"), or the `id` ("mesh:3") of a procedural mesh a script made with mesh.create() (it lives as long as the scene: a scene load releases it). |
| `texture` | asset (texture) | `""` | Base color texture. Empty = none (or the glTF material). "target:<name>" shows the live picture of the Camera whose `renderTarget` is that name (a screen, a mirror, the page of a book; docs/RENDERING.md, "Render targets"). A pointer over the mesh reaches the Interactables of that camera. |
| `normalMap` | asset (texture) | `""` | Tangent-space normal map (glTF convention: +Y up, the usual blue-ish image) that adds small-scale relief without more triangles. Empty = none (or the glTF material's normalTexture). Replaces the glTF one when set. Takes "target:<name>" like `texture`. (since 0.2.0) |
| `normalScale` | float | `1.0` | How strong the normal map is: 0 = flat, 1 = as authored. Range 0.0..4.0. (since 0.2.0) |
| `color` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]` | Base color, multiplied with the texture. |
| `metallic` | float | `0.0` | 0 = plastic/stone, 1 = metal. glTF models use their own metallic value and metallicRoughnessTexture instead. Range 0.0..1.0. |
| `roughness` | float | `0.6` | 0 = mirror-smooth, 1 = fully rough/matte. glTF models use their own roughness and metallicRoughnessTexture instead. Range 0.0..1.0. |
| `emissive` | color | `[0.0,0.0,0.0,1.0]` | Light emitted by the surface regardless of lighting (glow). Black = none. |
| `unlit` | bool | `false` | true = ignore lighting and draw the flat base color. |
| `castShadows` | bool | `true` | Cast shadows from shadow-casting lights. |
| `receiveShadows` | bool | `true` | Receive shadows from shadow-casting lights. |
| `uvScale` | vec2 | `[1.0,1.0]` | Texture tiling [u, v]; 2 repeats the texture twice. |
| `material` | asset (material) | `""` | Project-relative path of a custom material, a *.material.json file (e.g. "materials/water.material.json"), or "" (default) for the standard PBR material. The material file names a GLSL snippet whose surface() changes what the standard material computed (albedo, alpha, normal, emission...) and whose optional vertex() moves the vertices, and declares its params, textures, lighting (pbr or unlit) and alphaMode (opaque, clip or blend). The `material.info` command lists a material's params and textures; `shader.compile` compiles it and reports errors with file:line. The material's alphaMode wins over color.a < 1; `unlit` true forces unlit lighting. A material that does not compile draws magenta and logs why. Guide with worked examples: docs/SHADERS.md (`factoria docs read shaders`). (since 0.2.0) |
| `materialParams` | json | `{}` | Per-entity overrides of the material's params and textures, as an object keyed by the name declared in the material file: numbers for float params, arrays for vectors and colors ([r, g, b, a]), project-relative paths for textures (a path, or "target:<name>" for the live picture of a render-target camera). Example: {"glow": [1, 0.2, 0, 1], "mask": "textures/leaf.png"}. Unnamed params keep the material's defaults. An entity without overrides batches with the others that share the material. (since 0.2.0) |
| `materialColors` | json | `{}` | Per-material colours of a glTF model, an object keyed by glTF material name: {"Body": [0.2, 0.8, 0.7, 1]}. The colour REPLACES that material's baseColorFactor on its sub-meshes (the texture still multiplies it) and `color` still multiplies the result, so `color` stays the tint of the whole model. Materials not named keep their own colour. Names come from the model (the sub-mesh keeps its material name from import); `factoria validate` checks them and suggests the right one for a typo. Ignored by built-in shapes. Entities that differ only in materialColors are drawn in separate batches. (since 0.3.0) |
| `lods` | json | `[]` | Lower-detail meshes the renderer swaps in with distance, an array ordered from the nearest: [{"mesh": "assets/models/lamp.lod1.glb", "distance": 12}, {"mesh": "assets/models/lamp.lod2.glb", "distance": 30}]. From the camera distance (metres, between the camera and the entity's origin) of an entry on, that mesh is drawn instead of `mesh`; farther entries win. `mesh` itself is the full-detail one. `model.bake` writes these files and the prefab that sets this field when a model document has gameReady.lods (docs/MODELING.md). An entry that is not an object with a `mesh` string and a `distance` number is ignored. Colliders and picking keep using `mesh`. Entities that differ only in their LOD are drawn in the batch of the mesh they show. (since 0.16.0) |

### Light

A light source for 3D meshes. A directional light shines along the entity's forward direction (-Z rotated by the Transform), point and spot lights shine from the entity's position.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `type` | enum: directional \\| point \\| spot | `"directional"` | directional: sun-like, infinite distance. point: radiates in all directions. spot: cone along forward. |
| `color` | color | `[1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0]` | Light color. |
| `intensity` | float | `1.0` | Brightness multiplier. Range 0.0..1000.0. |
| `range` | float | `10.0` | Point/spot only: distance in meters where the light fades to zero. Range 0.01..100000.0. |
| `spotAngle` | float | `30.0` | Spot only: cone half-angle in degrees. Range 1.0..89.0. |
| `castShadows` | bool | `false` | Cast shadows. Only supported on directional lights for now. |

### Animator

Since 0.2.0.

Plays animation clips: the skeletal clips of a skinned glTF model (the model of the MeshRenderer on the same entity, or `model`), or, when there is no glTF model, the keyframed 2D clips of `clips` (*.anim.json files that animate fields of this entity and its children: position, rotation.z, color.a, Sprite.region...). One clip at a time with cross-fades, clip events, an optional small state machine (`params`, `states`, `transitions`) and, for 2D clips, `layers`. It runs in the fixed step, so headless runs and replays match. Scripts: entity.animator.play("Run", 0.2), .set("speed", 3), .stop(); events reach world.on(name, ...).

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `model` | string | `""` | Project-relative .gltf/.glb path with the skin and the clips. Empty = the `mesh` of the MeshRenderer on the same entity (usual case: leave it empty). |
| `clip` | string | `""` | Name of the clip playing now: a glTF animation, or a key of `clips` (see entity.animator.clips). Assigning it at run time switches clips with a cross-fade of `fade` seconds. Empty = bind pose (the model as exported), or, for 2D clips, the fields rest where they were before the first clip drove them. |
| `clips` | json | `{}` | Clip files, an object name -> project-relative *.anim.json path, such as {"walk": "anim/hero_walk.anim.json", "idle": "anim/hero_idle.anim.json"}. Two kinds (docs/ANIMATION.md). 2D clips ("2D clips") are used when the Animator has no glTF `model` (and the MeshRenderer on the entity is not a glTF): they animate fields of this entity and its descendants (found by EntityInfo name), a runtime pose that scene.save does not write. 3D bone clips (format factoria.anim3d/1, "3D bone clips") are used when the Animator plays a skinned glTF (a rig.bake .glb): they pose its bones, and sit next to the model's own animations. `clip`, `states` and play() name these either way. (since 0.7.0) |
| `speed` | float | `1.0` | Playback speed multiplier: 1 = authored speed, 2 = twice as fast, 0 = frozen. Range 0.0..100.0. |
| `loop` | bool | `true` | true = start over when the clip ends. false = stop on the last pose and send the `anim.finished` event. |
| `playing` | bool | `true` | Set false to pause, true to play. |
| `fade` | float | `0.2` | Cross-fade seconds used when `clip` is changed by assignment (play() takes its own). Range 0.0..60.0. |
| `params` | json | `{}` | State machine parameters and their start values, an object such as {"speed": 0, "grounded": true}. Numbers and booleans. Scripts change them with animator.set(name, value); transitions read them. |
| `states` | json | `{}` | State machine states, an object name -> {clip, loop (default true), speed (default 1), onEnter}. `onEnter` is the name of a game event sent when the state starts (world.on). Example: {"idle": {"clip": "Idle"}, "run": {"clip": "Run", "onEnter": "started_running"}}. |
| `transitions` | json | `[]` | State machine transitions, an array checked in order every step; the first that matches fires. Each: {from (a state, or "*"/omitted = any), to, when, fade (seconds, default 0.2), onFinish}. `when` is conditions joined by "&&": `speed > 0.1`, `grounded`, `!grounded`, `hp <= 0` (operators > >= < <= == !=). A parameter set with animator.trigger(name) is true for one step. onFinish: true fires when the current non-looping clip ended (alone or together with `when`). |
