| `fromBar` | integer | no | First bar shown in the picture (default 1). |
| `bars` | integer | no | Number of bars shown (default: to the end). |

### `music.check`

Since 0.16.0.

Find what is wrong in a song before listening: notes outside the key or the instrument's range, clashes, mud, silent tracks, loudness.

Runs the music checks on a song (`path` or inline `song`). Rules: off_key (a note outside the song's key and mode that is not a passing tone), range (a note outside the instrument's range or the track's `range`), clash (a minor second or a tritone sounding together on a strong beat), mud (close low notes under C3), structure (a track that never plays, an empty section, an unused pattern) and loudness (the song is rendered with its mixer: with the master limiter off a clipping mix is an error and a peak over -1 dBFS a warning; a limiter that pulls the level down by more than 6 dB is a warning, more than 3 dB a note; a mix below -35 LUFS is a warning; an integrated loudness more than 3 LU from the target is a warning, unless the master `loudness` brings it there). Without `rules` every rule that needs no render runs; `render: true` adds loudness. The target is `targetLufs`, else style.audio.loudnessLufs.music of assets.json when the style guide says it. Every finding has the rule, severity, a message, a fix (`hint`), the track, pattern, section, bar and position, and for a note the pointer, line, column and token in the note text; equal findings are reported once with a `count`. `ok` is true when there is no error and no warning. A song with mistakes fails like music.info. Example: {"path":"assets/music/theme.song.json","render":true}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | no | The song, project-relative, under assets/ and ending in .song.json, e.g. "assets/music/theme.song.json". |
| `song` | object | no | The song itself, as JSON, to check before writing it to a file. |
| `rules` | array | no | Which rules to run (default: every rule that needs no render). Naming loudness renders the song. |
| `render` | boolean | no | Also run the loudness rule: render the song and measure it. Default false. |
| `targetLufs` | number | no | Integrated loudness the music should have (LUFS, -70 to 0). Default: style.audio.loudnessLufs.music of assets.json, if set. |

### `music.chord`

Since 0.16.0.

Spell a chord by name, or a chord progression in a key: notes, MIDI numbers and the note text to paste.

With `name` ("Am7", "Cmaj7/G", "F#dim", "Dsus4") it returns the chord's notes at `octave`, their MIDI numbers, the interval list and the two ways to write it in note text. With `progression` (names, or Roman numerals in `key` and `mode`, or those of the song at `path`) it returns every chord and `pad`, the progression as sustained chords. With no arguments it lists the chord qualities the notation knows. Example: {"progression":"i VI III VII","key":"A","mode":"minor"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | no | One chord: root, quality, optional /bass. Omit to list qualities. |
| `progression` | string | no | Chord names or Roman numerals; *N holds a chord N bars. |
| `path` | string | no | Read meter, key and mode from this song. |
| `key` | string | no | Key for Roman numerals. Default C, or the song's. |
| `mode` | string | no | Scale for Roman numerals. Default major, or the song's. |
| `meter` | string | no | Meter such as "4/4". Default 4/4, or the song's. |
| `octave` | integer | no | Octave of the chord's root (C4 is middle C). Default 3. |

### `music.create` (modifies state)

Since 0.16.0.

Write a new song document: pad, bass, drums and an arpeggio over a chord progression, with intro, loop and outro.

Makes a complete, valid starting song at `path` (assets/..., ending in .song.json): a pad playing the chords, a bassline, a drum groove in a style and (unless arpeggio is false) a plucked arpeggio; sections intro, loop (twice) and outro. It is a starting point to change with music.edit, not a finished piece. `progression` is chord names ("Am F C G") or Roman numerals in the key ("i VI III VII"; `*2` holds a chord two bars). Defaults: tempo from the drum style's usual range, 4/4, key A minor, progression "i VI III VII" (minor) or "I V vi IV" (major), style rock (waltz in 3/4), bass root_fifth. Fails with `exists` when the file is there unless overwrite is true. Returns the song's summary and a piano-roll picture (`$image`). Example: {"path":"assets/music/theme.song.json","key":"D","mode":"dorian","tempo":96,"style":"funk"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | The song, project-relative, under assets/ and ending in .song.json, e.g. "assets/music/theme.song.json". |
| `picture` | boolean | no | Return the piano-roll picture (`$image`) of the new song. Default true. |
| `tempo` | number | no | Quarter notes per minute, 20 to 400. Default: the middle of the drum style's usual range. |
| `meter` | string | no | Meter such as "4/4", "3/4" or "6/8". Default 4/4. |
| `key` | string | no | Key, a note name such as "A", "F#" or "Bb". Default A. |
| `mode` | string | no | Scale: major, minor, dorian, phrygian, lydian, mixolydian, ... (music.scale lists them). Default minor. |
| `progression` | string | no | Chords by name ("Am F C G", "Am7 \| Fmaj7") or Roman numerals in the key ("i VI III VII"); *N holds a chord N bars. Default: the usual four chords of the mode. |
| `style` | string | no | Drum style (music.drums lists them): rock, funk, waltz, ... Default rock, or waltz in 3/4. |
| `bassStyle` | string | no | Bassline style: root, root_fifth, octave or walking. Default root_fifth. |
| `arpeggio` | boolean | no | Add a plucked arpeggio track. Default true. |
| `swing` | number | no | Swing from 0 (straight) to 1 (triplet feel). |
| `doc` | string | no | A sentence about the song, stored in the document. |
| `seed` | integer | no | The song's seed (the take of random hits and arpeggios). |
| `overwrite` | boolean | no | Replace the file when it exists. Default false. |
| `pictureOut` | string | no | Also keep the picture's PNG at this project path (ends in .png). |
| `width` | integer | no | Width of the picture in pixels (default 1000). |
| `fromBar` | integer | no | First bar shown in the picture (default 1). |
| `bars` | integer | no | Number of bars shown (default: to the end). |

### `music.edit` (modifies state)

Since 0.16.0.

Change a song document: tempo, tracks, patterns, sections, the arrangement, mutes and automation, checked before anything is written.

Applies `ops` in order to the song at `path` and writes it, but only if the result is a valid song (otherwise it fails with `invalid_song`, every problem in data.issues, and the file is untouched). Each op is an object with `op` and its fields: set_song {tempo, meter, key, mode, swing, swingGrid, seed, volume, doc} (null removes a field); add_track {track, instrument, volume, pan, mute, solo, voices, effects, sends, transpose, swing, range, kit, patterns, automation, play}; set_track {track, name (renames and updates the sections), instrument (a name, a .sfx.json, "x.sf2#Preset" or {soundfont, preset, bank}), volume, pan, mute, solo, voices, effects, sends, transpose, swing, range, kit, automation} (null removes); set_mixer {buses: {name: {volume, pan, mute, effects} | null}, master: {effects, limiter, loudness}} (docs/MUSIC.md "Mixer"; a bus merges field by field, null removes a bus or a field); set_layers {layers: {name: [tracks] | {tracks, intensity, doc} | null}} (the groups of tracks music.render writes as stems and a layered player brings in; docs/MUSIC.md "Layers"); remove_track {track} (and every mention in the sections); set_pattern {track, pattern, notes (note text, or a list of {pitch, tick, duration, velocity, accent, staccato} that is written as note text) | grid+step+bars, play}; remove_pattern {track, pattern} (and its uses in the sections); add_section {section, kind (intro, loop, outro, section), repeat, bars, mute, play, index}; set_section {section, name, kind, repeat, bars, mute, play} (play changes only the tracks named, null stops one); remove_section {section}; move_section {section, index}; arrange {section, track, entries} ("a a b*2 rest", a list, or null to stop the track in that section); mute {section, tracks, muted}; set_automation {track (omit for the whole song), param (volume, pan, filter, macro.<name>), points [[beat, value], ...], curve (linear, step, smooth)} (no points removes the lane). `play` in add_track and set_pattern is {section: entries} to place the pattern at once. Note text is in docs/MUSIC.md. Returns the song's summary and what each op did. Example: {"path":"assets/music/theme.song.json","ops":[{"op":"set_pattern","track":"bass","pattern":"line","notes":"A2:8 A2 E3 A2 | G2:8 G2 D3 G2"},{"op":"mute","section":"intro","tracks":["drums"]}]}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | The song, project-relative, under assets/ and ending in .song.json, e.g. "assets/music/theme.song.json". |
| `ops` | array | yes | The operations, applied in order. |
| `picture` | boolean | no | Return the piano-roll picture (`$image`) of the song after the change. Default false. |
| `pictureOut` | string | no | Also keep the picture's PNG at this project path (ends in .png). |
| `width` | integer | no | Width of the picture in pixels (default 1000). |
| `fromBar` | integer | no | First bar shown in the picture (default 1). |
| `bars` | integer | no | Number of bars shown (default: to the end). |

### `music.export_midi` (modifies state)

Since 0.16.0.

Write a song as a format-1 Standard MIDI File that a DAW or notation program opens.

Writes the song at `path` as a Standard MIDI File (format 1, 960 ticks per quarter note) at `out` (default: the song's path with .mid). Track 1 holds the tempo, time signature, key signature (major or minor) and one marker per section ("kind:name"); then one track per song track with its name, instrument (Instrument Name and the General MIDI program), volume and pan controllers and its notes with the length they sound; drum tracks use channel 10 and the General MIDI percussion keys. The sounded timeline is written: swing is in the note times, `transpose` in the pitches, and muted tracks (or tracks not soloed) are left out. The mixer, effects, buses and automation are not part of a MIDI file. music.import_midi reads the file back as the same notes, timing and velocities. Example: {"path":"assets/music/theme.song.json"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | The song, project-relative, under assets/ and ending in .song.json. |
| `out` | string | no | The MIDI file to write: a project path ending in .mid. Default: the song's path with .mid. |
| `overwrite` | boolean | no | Replace the file when it exists. Default false. |

### `music.import_midi` (modifies state)

Since 0.16.0.

Turn a Standard MIDI File (.mid) into a song document: tracks, patterns, sections from markers, drums as grids.

Reads the MIDI file `path` (absolute on this machine, or in the project) with the engine's own parser (format 0 and 1, running status, meta events, any number of tracks and channels; format 2 and SMPTE timing are errors) and writes a song document at `out` (default assets/music/<name>.song.json; assets.import does the same for a .mid). Every (track, channel, program) that plays notes becomes a song track: channel 10 is a drum track (General MIDI percussion keys become the lanes of the built-in kit, as a step grid with ghost / hit / accent velocities), the others take the built-in instrument nearest to the General MIDI program (an Instrument Name that names a built-in instrument wins; with `soundfont` the track plays that SoundFont's preset of the program). Velocities are kept, the sustain pedal lengthens notes, controllers 7 and 10 become the track's volume and pan. `quantize` ("off" keeps the written times to 1/48 of a quarter note; "16", "8t", "32"...) snaps starts and ends. Markers become sections (a name starting with intro, loop or outro, or written "loop:name"); without markers the song is one section `main`, a loop when `loop` is true. Repeated bars of a track become one pattern played several times. Tempo, meter and key come from the first such event; a later change cannot be held by a song and is listed in `warnings`. Errors name the byte offset in the file. The result is the song summary (as music.info) plus `import` (what was read) and `warnings`; `license`, `author` and `sourceUrl` go to the song's provenance in assets.json. An existing song is an `exists` error unless overwrite is true. Example: {"path":"C:/music/theme.mid","out":"assets/music/theme.song.json","quantize":"16"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | The MIDI file: an absolute path on this machine, or relative to the project. Ends in .mid or .midi. |
| `out` | string | no | The song to write: under assets/, ending in .song.json. Default: assets/music/<name>.song.json. |
| `quantize` | string | no | "off" (default) or a note value to snap starts and ends to: "4", "8", "16", "32", "64", "8t", "16t"... |
| `soundfont` | string | no | A SoundFont (.sf2) under assets/: pitched tracks play its preset with their General MIDI program and drums its drum kit. |
| `loop` | boolean | no | A file with no markers: make its one section the song's loop (default: an ordinary section). Default false. |
| `overwrite` | boolean | no | Replace the song when it exists. Default false. |
| `license` | string | no | License of the MIDI file ("CC0", "CC-BY 4.0"), for the credits. |
| `author` | string | no | Who made the MIDI file. |
| `sourceUrl` | string | no | The page the file came from, for the credits. |

### `music.info`

Since 0.16.0.

Check a song document and say what it holds: structure, bars, seconds, a summary per section, and a piano-roll picture.

Reads a song (`*.song.json`, format factoria.song/1, docs/MUSIC.md and schemas/song.schema.json) from `path`, or takes it inline as `song`, and checks it. A song with mistakes fails with `invalid_song` and EVERY problem in data.issues (JSON pointer, line and column inside note text, what is wrong and how to fix it), so one call is enough to repair it. A valid song returns tempo, meter, key, mode, swing, the length in bars and seconds, the structure ("intro (4 bars) > loop (8 bars) x2 > outro (4 bars)"), each track (instrument, patterns and their bars, notes played, the range they cover, the sections they play in) and each section (kind, bars, repeats, what every track plays, where it starts in bars and seconds, notes per bar and per track), and where its preview WAV is and whether it is stale. Unless `picture` is false it also returns a piano roll (`$image`): the sections on top, one colour per track, brighter = louder, drum lanes below; `fromBar` and `bars` zoom on a part. Example: {"path":"assets/music/theme.song.json"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | no | The song, project-relative, under assets/ and ending in .song.json, e.g. "assets/music/theme.song.json". |
| `song` | object | no | The song itself, as JSON, to check before writing it to a file (format is filled in). |
| `picture` | boolean | no | Return the piano-roll picture (`$image`). Default true. |
| `pictureOut` | string | no | Also keep the picture's PNG at this project path (ends in .png). Default: a temporary screenshot. |
| `width` | integer | no | Width of the picture in pixels (default 1000). |
| `fromBar` | integer | no | First bar shown in the picture (default 1). |
| `bars` | integer | no | Number of bars shown (default: to the end). |

### `music.instrument` (modifies state)

Since 0.16.0.

List the built-in song instruments (by family), the drum kits and lanes, sfx presets and project SoundFonts, show the patch behind an instrument, or list a SoundFont's presets.

Without `name` it lists what a track's `instrument` can be: the built-in pitched instruments (with family, note range and polyphony), the drum kits (acoustic "kit", "kit:electronic", "kit:chiptune") and their lanes ("kit:kick"), the sfx presets, the .sfx.json patches and the .sf2 SoundFonts in the project. With `name` set to a .sf2 path under assets/ it lists that SoundFont's presets (name, bank, program) so a track can name one. With `name` set to a built-in it returns that instrument's patch (the JSON of a .sfx.json, docs/SOUND.md; a bare lane name like "kick" works) and, with `path`, writes it to a .sfx.json under assets/ so you can change the numbers and point a track at the copy. A pitched patch is played once per note, re-pitched to the note. Example: {"name":"pluck","path":"assets/audio/my_pluck.sfx.json"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | no | A built-in instrument ("pluck"), a drum lane ("kit:kick", "kit:electronic:kick" or "kick") or a project .sf2 ("assets/audio/piano.sf2": lists its presets). Omit to list them all. |
| `path` | string | no | Write the patch here (a .sfx.json under assets/). |
| `overwrite` | boolean | no | Replace the file at `path` when it exists. Default false. |

### `music.mix`

Since 0.16.0.

Render a song in memory and report the mix: each track's level, the buses and what the master's loudness normalization and limiter did.

Renders the song (`path`, or inline `song`) like music.preview but writes no file, and returns the mix: for every track its notes, peak (dBFS) and loudness (LUFS) as heard in the mix, volume, pan, effects and sends; the buses (volume, pan, effects); and the master: the loudness and peak before the loudness gain and the limiter, the gain the normalization added, the target loudness (`mixer.master.loudness`: "style" is the project's style.audio.loudnessLufs.music, a number is LUFS, "off" leaves the level), whether the limiter is on and how many dB it pulled down at most. Use it to balance the tracks (a track 10 LU above the others covers them), to see whether the limiter is squashing a hot mix, and before music.edit set_track / set_mixer. `fromBar`, `bars`, `solo`, `mute`, `seed` and `sampleRate` work as in music.preview. Example: {"path":"assets/music/theme.song.json","bars":8}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | no | The song, project-relative, under assets/ and ending in .song.json. |
| `song` | object | no | The song document inline (a song not saved yet); `path` or `song`. |
| `fromBar` | integer | no | First bar rendered, counted from 1 (default 1). |
| `bars` | integer | no | Number of bars rendered from `fromBar` (default: to the end). |
| `solo` | array | no | Render only these tracks. |
| `mute` | array | no | Leave these tracks out. |
| `seed` | integer | no | Added to the song's seed. Default 0. |
| `sampleRate` | integer [22050,32000,44100,48000] | no | Sample rate of the render (22050 is faster). Default 44100. |

### `music.notes`

Since 0.16.0.

List the notes of one pitched pattern of a song (pitch, tick, duration, velocity), or the hits of a drum pattern, as a piano roll sees them.

Reads the pattern `pattern` of `track` in the song at `path` and returns its notes sorted by start: `pitch` (MIDI, 60 is C4), `name`, `tick` and `duration` (960 ticks per quarter note, from the start of the pattern), `velocity`, `accent` and `staccato`; a chord is one note per pitch. `text` is the note text as written. The list goes back through music.edit set_pattern with `notes` as a list (changing, adding or removing notes), which writes it as note text again. A drum pattern returns its `grid` and `hits`. Example: {"path":"assets/music/theme.song.json","track":"bass","pattern":"line"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | The song, project-relative, under assets/ and ending in .song.json, e.g. "assets/music/theme.song.json". |
| `track` | string | yes | The track. |
| `pattern` | string | yes | The pattern of that track. |

### `music.preview` (modifies state)

Since 0.16.0.

Render a song to a stereo WAV or OGG next to it (offline, deterministic) and see its spectrogram.

Renders the song at `path` with the preview voices: every note of the arrangement is played by its track's instrument at the note's pitch (a built-in instrument, a preset, or your own .sfx.json patch), with the track's volume, pan, swing and automation lanes and the song's master lanes. The result is a stereo 16-bit WAV at `out` (default: the song's path with .preview.wav; a path ending in .ogg encodes Ogg Vorbis). No provider, no key, no other program: the same song, options and seed give the same bytes on every platform. The file gets provenance and a recipe in assets.json whose inputs are the song and every patch it read, so project.validate warns when they changed after the preview was made and assets.regenerate renders it again. `fromBar` and `bars` render a part, `solo` and `mute` choose tracks, `seed` is another take of the instruments' noise, `sampleRate` 22050, 32000, 44100 (default) or 48000. A song longer than 180 s needs a range. An existing file that music.preview did not make is an `exists` error unless overwrite is true. The result has the measurements (lufs, peakDb), the numbers of the file as written (`analysis`) and the spectrogram picture (`$image`). The song's mixer applies: track effects and sends, the buses, the master limiter and the loudness normalization to the style's music loudness; `mix` in the result says what each did (music.mix gives the same without writing a file). Example: {"path":"assets/music/theme.song.json","fromBar":5,"bars":4,"solo":["lead"]}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | The song, project-relative, under assets/ and ending in .song.json, e.g. "assets/music/theme.song.json". |
| `out` | string | no | Where to write the sound: .wav or .ogg under assets/. Default: the song's path with .preview.wav. |
| `fromBar` | integer | no | First bar rendered, counted from 1 (default 1). Notes that start earlier are not played. |
| `bars` | integer | no | Number of bars rendered from `fromBar` (default: to the end). |
| `solo` | array | no | Render only these tracks. |
| `mute` | array | no | Leave these tracks out. |
| `seed` | integer | no | Added to the song's seed: another take of the instruments' noise. The same seed always gives the same file. Default 0. |
| `sampleRate` | integer [22050,32000,44100,48000] | no | Sample rate of the file. Default 44100. |
| `overwrite` | boolean | no | Replace the file when it exists and was not made by music.preview (one made by it is always replaced). Default false. |
| `picture` | boolean | no | Return the spectrogram picture (`$image`) of the preview. Default true. |
| `pictureOut` | string | no | Also keep the picture's PNG at this project path (ends in .png). |
| `width` | integer | no | Width of the picture in pixels (default 1000). |
| `height` | integer | no | Height of the picture in pixels (default 640). |

### `music.render` (modifies state)

Since 0.16.0.

Render a whole song (intro, loop, outro) to a game-ready WAV or OGG with sample-exact loop points, and optionally one stem per layer.

Renders the song at `path` as music.preview does (same voices, mixer, loudness normalization and limiter) but as an ASSET: the whole song, with the loop points of its `loop` sections. The loop is seamless: the tail of the loop's last bar (reverb, release) is folded onto its first bar, so a looping AudioSource plays `loopStart`..`loopEnd` with no click. The points are the bar boundaries of the loop sections, exact frames, written as `import.loopStart` / `loopEnd` (seconds) in assets.json, which the engine honours, and, for a WAV, in the standard `smpl` chunk; an OGG keeps them in assets.json only. `out` (default: the song's path with .wav) or `format` "wav" / "ogg" choose the file. `stems`: "layers" renders one file per layer of the song's `layers` (the tracks left out form the layer `other`), "tracks" one per track, "buses" the dry tracks and each bus's return; true means "layers". A stem is named <out without extension>.stem.<name>.<ext>, has the same length, sample rate and loop points as the mix, and passes through the same buses and master: the stems carry the mix's loudness gain and limiter gain, so their SUM is the mix to within float rounding (below -80 dBFS) when the buses and the master hold only linear effects; a compressor, distortion or bitcrush there acts on the sum and the result's stemSum says by how much the sum differs. Add them with gain 1 and clip nothing: a stem can pass 0 dBFS when the others cancel it. Every written file gets provenance and the same recipe in assets.json (inputs: the song, every .sfx.json patch and SoundFont it reads; context: the style guide's music loudness when the song's master loudness is "style"), so project.validate warns when any of them changed and assets.regenerate makes the files again; running music.render again updates them in place (a stem of a layer you removed is deleted). `import.music` of each entry says what it is: {role: "mix", song, stemGrouping, stems: [{name, path, kind, intensity, tracks, buses}]} or {role: "stem", song, mix, name, kind, intensity, tracks, buses}; intensity (0..1) is when a layered player brings the stem in. `sampleRate` 22050, 32000, 44100 (default, exact loop frames in the engine) or 48000; `seed` another take of the instruments' noise; `loop` false renders the song once with no loop points. An existing file that music.render did not make is an `exists` error unless overwrite is true. Example: {"path":"assets/music/theme.song.json","stems":"layers"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | yes | The song, project-relative, under assets/ and ending in .song.json. |
| `out` | string | no | Where to write the mix: .wav or .ogg under assets/. Default: the song's path with .wav (or .ogg when `format` says so). |
| `format` | string ["wav","ogg"] | no | File format when `out` is not given. wav is lossless and holds the loop points in a smpl chunk; ogg is smaller. |
| `sampleRate` | integer [22050,32000,44100,48000] | no | Sample rate of the files. Default 44100. |
| `seed` | integer | no | Added to the song's seed: another take of the instruments' noise. Default 0. |
| `loop` | boolean | no | Find the song's loop sections, fold their tail onto the start and write the loop points. False: render once, no points. Default true. |
| `stems` | any | no | One file per stem: "layers" (the song's `layers`), "tracks" or "buses"; true = "layers"; false or absent: only the mix. |
| `overwrite` | boolean | no | Replace files that exist and were not made by music.render (the ones it made are always replaced). Default false. |

### `music.scale`

Since 0.16.0.

Say which notes a scale or mode has and the chords built on its degrees (with Roman numerals).

With `key` and `mode` returns the scale's notes, intervals, and the triads and seventh chords on every degree labelled with Roman numerals (the same names a progression accepts). With no arguments it lists every scale the notation knows. Example: {"key":"D","mode":"dorian"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `key` | string | no | Tonic, a note name such as "A" or "Bb". Default C. |
| `mode` | string | no | Scale name: major, minor, dorian, ... Default major. |

## physics

### `nav.bake`

Since 0.3.0.

Bake the NavMesh3D walkable grid from the static 3D colliders and return its stats.

A NavMesh3D component marks a box of the level. Baking voxelizes the static colliders inside it (no RigidBody3D or a static one; triggers, Collider3D.navObstacle and Collider3D.navWalkable colliders are left out; navWalkable ones are added as moving cells) into a grid of walkable cells: not steeper than maxSlope, agentHeight of room above, agentRadius from walls and drops, neighbours joined when they differ by at most stepHeight. It is baked by itself when the scene loads and when the colliders change (autoBake); call this to bake on demand, for example with autoBake off. mesh = id of the entity with the NavMesh3D; omitted = every enabled one. Result: a list of {mesh, cellsX, cellsZ, cells, spans, walkableCells, regions, obstacles, links, walkableBodies}; NavLink3D entities add off-mesh links; no timing, so the same level gives the same result. Example: nav.bake {"mesh":"navmesh"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mesh` | string | no | Id of the entity with the NavMesh3D to bake; omitted = all enabled ones. |

### `nav.find_path`

Since 0.3.0.

Find a walkable path between two 3D points on the baked NavMesh3D.

A* over the walkable grid, then string pulling: the result is few corner points from `from` to `to` on the walkable surface (meters). Result {found:true, points:[[x,y,z],...], length, complete, links?:[{point, entity}], from, to, mesh} or {found:false, reason, message, hint}: reason is start_off_mesh / goal_off_mesh (not on walkable ground; nearest and nearestDistance say where the nearest walkable point is) or disconnected (the two are in different walkable areas, a moving obstacle blocks the way, or a navWalkable platform is away). A start or goal within `snap` meters of walkable ground is moved onto it. closest=true returns a path to the reachable point nearest the goal (complete=false) instead of failing when disconnected. radius = agent radius of this query; larger than the NavMesh3D.agentRadius it was baked for is an error: bake for the bigger agent (a second NavMesh3D). mesh = id of the NavMesh3D entity; omitted = the first enabled one that contains `from`. Scripts: nav.findPath(from, to, {radius}). Example: nav.find_path {"from":[0,0,0],"to":[10,0,5]}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `from` | array | yes | Start point [x,y,z] in meters (the agent's feet). |
| `to` | array | yes | Goal point [x,y,z] in meters. |
| `radius` | number | no | Agent radius for this query; must not exceed NavMesh3D.agentRadius. Default: the mesh's. |
| `snap` | number | no | How far (meters) a start or goal off the walkable cells is moved onto the nearest one. Default: agentRadius + 2 cells. |
| `closest` | boolean | no | When the goal is unreachable, return a path to the reachable point nearest to it (complete=false). |
| `mesh` | string | no | Id of the entity with the NavMesh3D to use. Default: the first enabled one that contains `from`. |

### `nav.find_tile_path`

Since 0.3.0.

Find a path over the cells of a Tilemap (or a plain cost grid) with A*.

Cells are (col, row), 0-based, row 0 = the top row. Pass `tilemap` (id of an entity with a Tilemap: tiles in solidTiles block, every other cell costs 1, `costs` {"<tile index>": cost | null} overrides per tile, null = blocked, key "-1" = empty cells) OR `grid` {width, height, cost: [..row-major..], origin?, cellSize?} (cost = the cost of entering a cell, >= 0; null or negative = blocked). Steps are 4-way; diagonals=true allows 8-way and a diagonal never cuts a corner (both cells it passes between must be open). The start cell is always allowed; a blocked goal fails with goal_blocked unless allowBlockedGoal=true (it is then entered at cost 1) or closest=true. closest=true returns the path to the reachable cell nearest the goal (complete=false) when the goal cannot be reached; maxNodes bounds the search (reason too_far). Result {found, complete, cells:[[col,row]..], points:[[x,y]..] (cell centres: WORLD positions for a tilemap, origin + (col+0.5, -(row+0.5)) * cellSize for a grid), cost, length} or {found:false, reason: start_off_map | goal_off_map | goal_blocked | blocked | too_far, message, hint}. Deterministic. Scripts: nav.findTilePath(map, from, to, opts); a script that asks many times on one map keeps it with nav.createGrid (the command is stateless: it reads the map you give it on every call). nav.flow_field is the one-to-many form. Example: nav.find_tile_path {"tilemap":"ground","from":[0,0],"to":[5,3],"diagonals":true}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tilemap` | string | no | Id of the entity with the Tilemap. Give this or `grid`. |
| `grid` | object | no | A plain grid: {width, height, cost: [width*height numbers, row-major, row 0 = top; null or negative = blocked], origin?: [x,y] top-left corner, cellSize?: number \| [w,h]}. |
| `from` | array | yes | Start cell [col,row]. |
| `to` | array | yes | Goal cell [col,row]. |
| `costs` | object | no | Tilemap only: cost of entering a cell by tile index, {"3": 2.5, "7": null}; null or negative blocks, a solid tile listed here is walkable. |
| `diagonals` | boolean | no | Allow 8-way steps (no corner cutting). Default false. |
| `maxNodes` | integer | no | Most cells the search expands before it gives up (too_far). Default 100000. |
| `closest` | boolean | no | Goal unreachable: return the path to the nearest reachable cell (complete=false). |
| `allowBlockedGoal` | boolean | no | A blocked goal cell can still be entered (cost 1). |

### `nav.flow_field`

Since 0.3.0.

Distance field over the cells of a Tilemap (or a plain cost grid) from one or more goal cells.

The cost of the cheapest route from every cell to the nearest goal, with the same rules as nav.find_tile_path (entering a cell costs its cost, 4-way or diagonals=true, no corner cutting, null or negative blocks). A blocked goal is entered at cost 1. Pass `tilemap` or `grid` like nav.find_tile_path, `goals` [[col,row],...] and optionally `from`. Result {width, height, distance: [width*height numbers, row-major, row 0 = top; null where no goal can be reached]} and, with `from`: {reachable, cost, next: [col,row] | null (the cell to walk to; null at a goal or when unreachable), path: [[col,row]...] (from `from` to the goal it reaches)}. Deterministic. Scripts: nav.flowField(grid, goals) keeps the field and answers field.stepToward(col, row) in O(1). Example: nav.flow_field {"tilemap":"ground","goals":[[9,4]],"from":[0,0]}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tilemap` | string | no | Id of the entity with the Tilemap. Give this or `grid`. |
| `grid` | object | no | A plain grid: {width, height, cost: [width*height numbers, row-major, row 0 = top; null or negative = blocked], origin?: [x,y], cellSize?: number \| [w,h]}. |
| `goals` | array | yes | Goal cells [[col,row],...]; at least one. |
| `from` | array | no | A cell to read the next step and the path for. |
| `costs` | object | no | Tilemap only: cost of entering a cell by tile index, {"3": 2.5, "7": null}; null or negative blocks. |
| `diagonals` | boolean | no | Allow 8-way steps (no corner cutting). Default false. |

### `nav.info`

Since 0.3.0.

List the NavMesh3D components with their bounds, agent size, bake state and stats.

Use it to check that a level was baked and how much of it is walkable. Result: a list of {mesh, enabled, autoBake, baked, error?, boundsMin, boundsMax, cellSize, agentRadius, agentHeight, stepHeight, maxSlope, staleSinceBake, stats} (stats include links and walkableBodies). staleSinceBake is true when the colliders changed after the last bake of a mesh with autoBake off (call nav.bake).

## project

### `perf.baseline` (modifies state)

Since 0.2.0.

Measure the game and write or refresh THIS runner's entry in its performance budget file (perf.json).

Measures like perf.measure (3 runs, median) and stores the result under runners.<runner> of the budget file, keeping the other runners' entries, the run settings and any "tolerance" already there. Run it once per kind of machine you want checked (the runner id is os-compiler-renderer, e.g. windows-msvc-d3d11-warp, linux-gcc-llvmpipe, macos-clang-metal-paravirtual; a Debug build adds -debug), and again when the game got heavier ON PURPOSE. A game sets its own budget the same way: `factoria call perf.baseline` writes <project>/perf.json, commit it, and `factoria call perf.check` (in CI it fails past the tolerance) checks it. File: {format:"factoria.perf/1", frames, scene?, input?, tolerance?: {cpuAvg:1.0 (ratio over the baseline), cpuP95:1.5, memory:0.1, drawCalls:0.1, entities:0.1, triangles:0.1, lights:0.1, textureMB:0.1, cpuSlackMs:1, memorySlackMB:8, textureSlackMB:1, countSlack:2}, budgets?: {maxTriangles, maxLights, maxTextureMB, maxDrawCalls, maxEntities} (absolute caps, see perf.check), runners: {<id>: sample}}. A limit is max(baseline*(1+ratio), baseline+slack). `tolerance` here sets the file's tolerances. Returns {file, runner, sample, created}. Example: {"frames":300,"input":"replays/play.json"}.

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `file` | string | no | Budget file, project-relative (or absolute). Default "perf.json". |
| `frames` | integer | no | Frames per run; stored in the file (default: the file's value, else 300). |
| `scene` | string | no | Start scene; stored in the file. |
| `input` | string | no | Project-relative input replay; stored in the file. |
| `repeats` | integer | no | Runs to take the median of. Default 3. |
| `tolerance` | object | no | Tolerances to store in the file: cpuAvg, cpuP95, memory, drawCalls, entities, triangles, lights, textureMB (ratios), cpuSlackMs, memorySlackMB, textureSlackMB, countSlack. |

### `perf.check`

Since 0.2.0.

Measure the game and fail when it costs more than its performance budget (perf.json) allows on this runner.

Measures with the settings of the budget file (frames, scene, input) and compares with runners.<this runner> of the file (see perf.baseline for the format and the tolerances). Memory, draw calls, entities, triangles, lights and texture memory (the last three only when the baseline has them) past their limit FAIL always. The file's "budgets" object ({maxTriangles, maxLights, maxTextureMB, maxDrawCalls, maxEntities}) or the `budgets` argument sets absolute caps that fail whatever the baseline says, also on a runner with no baseline. A time (cpuMsAvg, cpuMsP95) past its limit FAILS when the CI environment variable is set; elsewhere it only WARNS (status "warn"), because a developer machine can be busy. A time over the limit is measured up to twice more (the best time of each metric counts) before it fails. A runner with no entry passes with status "no_baseline" and returns `baselineEntry`: the exact JSON to add under "runners" (or run perf.baseline here); with requireBaseline it fails instead (error `perf_no_baseline`, same data). Returns {runner, status: pass|warn|no_baseline, file, sample, rows: [{metric, measured, baseline, limit, exceeded}], message, baselineEntry?}; a failure is an error `perf_budget_exceeded` with the same data. Example: {} or {"file":"perf.json"}.

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `file` | string | no | Budget file, project-relative (or absolute). Default "perf.json". |
| `strictTime` | boolean | no | Make a time over its limit fail even outside CI (default: only in CI). |
| `requireBaseline` | boolean | no | Fail when this runner has no entry in the file, so a CI job cannot pass without checking anything. Default false. |
| `budgets` | object | no | Absolute caps that fail whatever the baseline says (they replace the same keys of the file's "budgets"): maxTriangles, maxLights, maxTextureMB, maxDrawCalls, maxEntities. |

### `perf.measure`

Since 0.2.0.

Run the game headless for N frames and report its cost: CPU time per frame, peak memory, draw calls, entities, triangles, lights, texture memory.

Runs the project in a second headless engine inside this process, drawing every frame with the GPU renderer when there is one (graphics "none" otherwise: draw calls are 0), and returns {runner, sample: {frames, cpuMsAvg, cpuMsP95, cpuMsMax (CPU time of the engine per frame: process CPU, not wall clock, so a busy machine moves it less), peakMemoryMB (peak resident memory of the process), drawCalls, entities, triangles (of the main pass), lights (3D lights of the main pass plus Light2D lights of the same frame) and textureMB (GPU texture memory), all max over the run, graphics}}. `runner` is the id of this machine's and build's kind (os-compiler-renderer, plus -debug for a Debug build, e.g. linux-gcc-llvmpipe) that budget files key their baselines by. `input` is an input replay (like `factoria run --input`) to reach the heavy part of the game. Peak memory is the whole process's, so measure with the same host every time (`factoria call --no-graphics perf.measure`). Example: {"frames":300}.

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `frames` | integer | no | How many frames to run (fixed step). Default 300. |
| `scene` | string | no | Start scene (default: the project's mainScene). |
| `input` | string | no | Project-relative input replay JSON applied during the run. |
| `repeats` | integer | no | Run this many times; time metrics are the median, memory/draw calls/entities the max. Default 1. |

### `perf.profile`

Since 0.2.0.

Run the game headless with the profiler on and report where the time goes: per engine system, per script behaviour class, GPU time, memory.

Use it when the game is slow and you need to know WHY (perf.measure only says how slow). Runs the project like perf.measure (drawing every frame with the GPU renderer when there is one) with the profiler on and returns {runner, graphics, profile}. profile = {frames, clock:"wall", frameMs:{avg,p95,max} (engine time of a frame), systems: {platform, physics, scriptsFixedUpdate, animation, scriptsEvents, ui, scriptsUpdate, audio, scriptsLateUpdate, localization, render, endOfFrame: {avgMs, p95Ms, maxMs}}, behaviours: [{class, path, avgMs (per frame, counting the frames it did not run), maxMs, callsPerFrame}] slowest first (every per-behaviour callback counts: onStart, onUpdate, onFixedUpdate, onLateUpdate, collision/trigger handlers, onEvent; timers, world.on handlers and promise jobs are the bucket "(timers, events and promises)"), gpu: {avgMs, p95Ms, maxMs, samples, reason} (milliseconds the GPU took to draw the world; null with a `reason` where the graphics backend has no timer queries: Metal, GLES3, WebGL2, or no GPU), memory: {start, end, peak: {processMB, jsHeapMB, textureMB, audioDecodedMB, entities}}}. Times are wall-clock milliseconds and vary a little from run to run: compare the ORDER and the big gaps, not the decimals. A system's time includes the behaviours it runs (scriptsUpdate holds every onUpdate). `warmup` frames (default 30) run first and are not counted, because the first frames load assets. Use `input` (an input replay) to reach the heavy part of the game. The profiler only measures: game.state, replays and saves are identical with it on. The editor's play sessions record the same section in play.report, and View > Profiler shows it live. Example: {"frames":300,"input":"replays/play.json"}.

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `frames` | integer | no | How many frames to profile (fixed step), after the warm-up. Default 300. |
| `warmup` | integer | no | Frames to run first and leave out of the numbers (assets load, caches fill). Default 30. |
| `scene` | string | no | Start scene (default: the project's mainScene). |
| `input` | string | no | Project-relative input replay JSON applied during the run. |

## physics

### `physics.raycast`

Cast a ray against colliders (2D segment or 3D ray) and return the first hit.

2D: {from:[x,y], to:[x,y]}. 3D: {dimension:"3d", origin:[x,y,z], direction:[x,y,z], maxDistance}. Options, the same as physics.shape_cast and the script API physics.raycast(a, b, {mask, ignore, ignoreTriggers}): mask = collision layer bit mask (bit i = layer i, -1 = all layers); ignore = id (or name) of an entity whose colliders, and its children's, are skipped (usually the caster, so a ray starting at a body's edge does not hit the body itself); ignoreTriggers (default true) skips trigger colliders, false hits them too. A collider that contains the ray origin is always skipped. Result: {hit:false} or {hit:true, entity, point, normal, distance}. Example: physics.raycast {"from":[0,300],"to":[0,-300],"ignore":"player","ignoreTriggers":false}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dimension` | string ["2d","3d"] | no |  Default "2d". |
| `from` | array | no | 2D start [x,y]. |
| `to` | array | no | 2D end [x,y]. |
| `origin` | array | no | 3D origin [x,y,z]. |
| `direction` | array | no | 3D direction. |
| `maxDistance` | number | no |  Default 1000. |
| `mask` | integer | no | Collision layer mask: bit i = layer i; -1 hits every layer. Default -1. |
| `ignore` | string | no | Entity id or name whose colliders (and its children's) are skipped, usually the caster. |
| `ignoreTriggers` | boolean | no | Skip trigger colliders; false hits them too. Default true. |

### `physics.raycast_all`

Since 0.3.0.

Cast a ray against colliders (2D segment or 3D ray) and return EVERY hit, nearest first.

Same arguments and options as physics.raycast, plus maxHits (default 32, the nearest ones are kept). Use it to see everything between two points (what hides a character from the camera), or to click through colliders that only exist to be faded. A collider with enabled=false is never reported. Result: {count, hits:[{entity, point, normal, distance}]} sorted by distance. Example: physics.raycast_all {"dimension":"3d","origin":[0,2,0],"direction":[0,0,-1],"maxDistance":20,"maxHits":4}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dimension` | string ["2d","3d"] | no |  Default "2d". |
| `from` | array | no | 2D start [x,y]. |
| `to` | array | no | 2D end [x,y]. |
| `origin` | array | no | 3D origin [x,y,z]. |
| `direction` | array | no | 3D direction. |
| `maxDistance` | number | no |  Default 1000. |
| `maxHits` | integer | no | At most this many hits (the nearest). Default 32. |
| `mask` | integer | no | Collision layer mask: bit i = layer i; -1 hits every layer. Default -1. |
| `ignore` | string | no | Entity id or name whose colliders (and its children's) are skipped, usually the caster. |
| `ignoreTriggers` | boolean | no | Skip trigger colliders; false hits them too. Default true. |

### `physics.shape_cast`

Sweep a circle, sphere or box from one point to another and return the first collider it touches.

Like physics.raycast, but the shape has size: use it to ask whether a character fits or how far a box can move before it hits something. 2 numbers in from/to = 2D, 3 numbers = 3D. shape: 2D {"shape":"circle","radius":8} or {"shape":"box","size":[16,24]}; 3D {"shape":"sphere","radius":0.5} or {"shape":"box","size":[1,2,1]} (2D pixels, 3D meters, full sizes). The shape is centred on the cast position and axis-aligned. Result: {hit:false} or {hit:true, entity, point, normal, distance}: distance is how far the CENTRE travels before contact, point the contact point, normal the hit surface's normal (pointing back at the shape). Colliders the shape already overlaps at `from` are skipped (like a ray starting inside one); a collider it only touches blocks the cast only if it moves towards it. Options as for physics.raycast: mask; ignore = id of an entity whose colliders (and its children's) are skipped, usually the caster; triggers are skipped unless ignoreTriggers=false. Example: physics.shape_cast {"shape":{"shape":"box","size":[32,48]},"from":[0,100],"to":[0,-300],"ignore":"player"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `shape` | object | yes | 2D: {shape:"circle",radius} or {shape:"box",size:[w,h]}. 3D: {shape:"sphere",radius} or {shape:"box",size:[x,y,z]}. |
| `from` | array | yes | Start of the shape's centre, [x,y] (2D) or [x,y,z] (3D). |
| `to` | array | yes | End of the shape's centre, same dimension as from. |
| `mask` | integer | no | Collision layer mask: bit i = layer i; -1 hits every layer. Default -1. |
| `ignore` | string | no | Entity id or name whose colliders (and its children's) are skipped, usually the caster. |
| `ignoreTriggers` | boolean | no | Skip trigger colliders; false hits them too. Default true. |

## platform

### `platform.add_backend` (modifies state)

Since 0.2.0.

Set up a store backend for this game: its plugin, its build and what the store needs.

One call instead of the manual steps of docs/PLATFORM.md ("Store backends"): writes the backend's plugin from its template (project.new_plugin with template = backend) unless factoria.json already declares it, builds it for this computer with CMake, and adds what that store needs. steam: the Steamworks plugin (achievements, stats, leaderboards, Cloud saves, DLC purchases, overlay, rich presence): writes it, builds it for this computer, copies Valve's redistributable libraries from the Steamworks SDK ("sdk": its folder or .zip) next to it for Windows, macOS and Linux, and writes steam_appid.txt ("appId", default Valve's test app 480) for development. apple: the StoreKit 2, Game Center and iCloud plugin for iOS and macOS (Swift: it builds on a Mac with Xcode). googleplay: the Google Play Billing, Play Games Services and Play Integrity plugin for Android (a C bridge and a Java module; it builds with the Android SDK's NDK). admob: the AdMob ads plugin for Android and iOS: Google's consent form (UMP), App Tracking Transparency on iOS and rewarded ads. It offers only the "ads" service, so it works next to the store backend of the game. Android: a C bridge and a Java module (built with the Android SDK's NDK). iOS: Swift (built on a Mac with Xcode against Google's iOS SDK: "sdk", its zip or folder). macOS has no AdMob SDK: there the game has no ads. Run it again after a change: it keeps what is there. Returns {backend, folder, done[], nextSteps[]}: nextSteps lists what only a person can do (store dashboards, accounts). factoria.json is patched, not rewritten: only the plugins.<backend> key is added, and the other keys, their order and the layout stay as they are. With `dryRun` true nothing is written, built or copied: the result is {backend, dryRun: true, folder, files[] (what it would write), keys[] (the factoria.json keys it would write), wouldDo[], nextSteps[]}. An argument that does not exist is an error with a "did you mean" (backend-specific ones like sdk or appId are listed above and are accepted for every backend). Example: {"backend": "steam", "appId": 480}.

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sdk` | string | no | (steam) The Steamworks SDK: its folder, or the steamworks_sdk_*.zip from partner.steamgames.com/downloads/list (a free Steamworks account). Valve's redistributable libraries are copied from it next to the plugin. Without it they are not copied: nextSteps says where to put them. Relative paths start in the project folder. (admob) Google's Mobile Ads SDK for iOS: its folder or the GoogleMobileAdsSdkiOS-*.zip from developers.google.com/admob/ios/quick-start. GoogleMobileAds.xcframework and UserMessagingPlatform.xcframework are copied from it into the plugin's ios/frameworks/ (git ignores them). Without it iOS is not built unless they are there already. Relative paths start in the project folder. |
| `appId` | integer | no | (steam) Your game's Steam app id, written to steam_appid.txt for development. Without it an existing steam_appid.txt is kept, else the file gets 480, Valve's test app (Spacewar), which any Steam account can run. |
| `appleSlices` | array | no | apple: which libraries to build: macos (the .dylib of a Mac app), iphoneos (an iPhone or iPad) and iphonesimulator (the iOS Simulator). Default: all three. |
| `appleBuild` | boolean | no | apple: false only writes the plugin and declares it, without building (any computer); build it later on a Mac with Xcode: cmake -S plugins/apple -B plugins/apple/build && cmake --build plugins/apple/build. Default true. |
| `playGamesId` | any | no | googleplay: the Play Games Services project id (digits: Play Console > Play Games Services > Setup and management > Configuration), written to android/src/main/res/values/games-ids.xml. Without it the backend offers purchases, the store page and Play Integrity, and no achievements, leaderboards or cloud saves. Kept as it is when not passed; "" turns Play Games off. Export again after changing it. |
| `googleplayBuild` | boolean | no | googleplay: false only writes the plugin and declares it, without building (any computer); build it later where the Android NDK is installed. Default true. |
| `admobBuild` | boolean | no | admob: false only writes the plugin and declares it, without building (any computer); build it later where the Android NDK (Android) or Xcode (iOS) is installed. Default true. |
| `admobPlatforms` | array | no | admob: the platforms the plugin is declared and built for. Default: android and ios. The iOS part is built only on a Mac. |
| `backend` | string ["steam","apple","googleplay","admob"] | yes | The store backend to set up; it is also the plugin's name. |
| `dryRun` | boolean | no | true = write, build and copy nothing: list the files and factoria.json keys it would write (files, keys) and the steps (wouldDo). Default false. |

### `platform.emit` (modifies state)

Since 0.2.0.

Send an event to the game as the store would: a purchase, the overlay opening or closing, a sign-in change.

`event` is "purchase" ({productId, status?: "purchased" | "pending" | "cancelled" (default purchased), transactionId?, receipt?}; a purchased one also records an unfinished transaction, made up when not given), "overlay" ({open: bool}) or "player" ({id?, name?, signedIn}). Scripts get it through platform.on(event, fn) at the start of the next frame (game.step). Fails when the game runs a real store backend. Example: platform.emit {"event":"overlay","data":{"open":true}}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `event` | string ["purchase","overlay","player"] | yes | The event name. |
| `data` | object | no | The event's data. Default {}. |

### `platform.remote_play_connect` (modifies state)

Since 0.3.0.

A guest joins the fake platform's Remote Play Together session, as Steam would tell the game.

Adds a session that remotePlay.sessions() lists and sends the game {status: "connected", session} at the start of the next frame (game.step), which platform.on("remotePlay", fn) listeners receive. `session` is {id (numbered from 1), guestName, guestId, deviceName, formFactor, resolution: {width, height}}; what you leave out is made up ("Guest 1", "fake-guest-1", "Fake device", "computer", 1920 x 1080). Returns the session. A guest's input is NOT simulated here: drive the pad the guest would use with game.gamepad(i). Fails when the game runs a real store backend. Example: platform.remote_play_connect {"guestName":"Ana","formFactor":"phone"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `guestName` | string | no | The guest's name on the store (Steam's persona name). |
| `guestId` | string | no | The guest's account id on the store (a SteamID as decimal text). |
| `deviceName` | string | no | The name of the guest's device. |
| `formFactor` | string ["unknown","phone","tablet","computer","tv","vr"] | no | The kind of device the guest plays on. |
| `resolution` | object | no | The guest's screen in pixels: {width, height}. |

### `platform.remote_play_disconnect` (modifies state)

Since 0.3.0.

A guest leaves the fake platform's Remote Play Together session.

Removes the session from remotePlay.sessions() and sends the game {status: "disconnected", session} (the session as it was) at the start of the next frame (game.step). Fails when no guest has that session id (the message lists the connected ones) or when the game runs a real store backend. Example: platform.remote_play_disconnect {"id":1}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | integer | yes | The session id platform.remote_play_connect returned. |

### `platform.reset` (modifies state)

Since 0.2.0.

Reset the fake platform backend: nothing unlocked, bought or saved, no scripted answers, signed in, an empty request log.

Also numbers transactions from fake-1 and integrity tokens from fake-integrity-1 again, and forgets the answer of platform.ads.setUnderAge (the game asks the age again). Pending requests are not cancelled. Fails when the game runs a real store backend (the message says which and why). Tests start every file with a fresh fake already; use this between tests that share state. Example: platform.reset {}

### `platform.respond` (modifies state)

Since 0.2.0.

Script the next answer(s) the fake platform backend gives to a method: an error, an exact result, or a change to the default.

`method` is a platform method such as "purchases.buy" (docs/PLATFORM.md lists them all). `answer` is one of {"error": "network", "message"?, "hint"?} to reject (codes: unavailable, notSignedIn, notAllowed, unknownId, network, failed), {"result": value} to resolve with exactly that value, or any other object, which is merged into the default result: {"status": "cancelled"} cancels a purchase (and buys nothing). Answers are used first in, first out, one per request; `times` queues the same answer several times. Fails when the game runs a real store backend. Example: platform.respond {"method":"purchases.buy","answer":{"status":"cancelled"}}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `method` | string | yes | The platform method, e.g. "purchases.buy", "achievements.unlock", "cloud.save". |
| `answer` | object | yes | {error, message?, hint?} \| {result} \| an object merged into the default result. |
| `times` | integer | no | How many requests get this answer. Default 1. |

### `platform.revoke` (modifies state)

Since 0.3.0.

Take a purchase back in the fake platform backend, as a refund does, and send the game the event a real store would.

The product leaves purchases.restore() and its unfinished transaction is dropped; the game gets a "purchase" event {status: "revoked", productId, transactionId, receipt} at the start of the next frame (game.step), which platform.on("purchase", fn) listeners receive. Fails when the player owns no such product (the message lists the owned ones) or when the game runs a real store backend. Example: platform.revoke {"productId":"remove_ads"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `productId` | string | yes | The catalog id of the product to take back, e.g. "remove_ads". |

### `platform.set_ad` (modifies state)

Since 0.3.0.

Script what the fake platform backend's test ad does: watched to the end, closed early, no ad to show, or consent refused.

`outcome` decides how every ads.showRewarded() ends until changed (and platform.reset): "watched" (the default: {rewarded: true}), "closedEarly" ({rewarded: false, reason: "closedEarly"}), "noFill" (no ad: ads.available() is false and showRewarded gives reason "noFill") or "consentRefused" (also sets gdpr and tracking to "denied"; reason "consentRefused"). `gdpr` ("granted", "denied", "notRequired", "unknown") and `tracking` ("authorized", "denied", "notDetermined", "restricted", "notRequired") are what ads.consent() answers; a denied gdpr stops every ad. `privacyOptions` ("required", "notRequired", "unknown") is what ads.consent() answers for the privacy options form: with "required", platform.ads.privacyOptions() "shows" the form. Give any of them. platform.state's fake.ads counts the ads shown and rewarded and the privacy forms shown. Fails when the game runs a real store backend. Example: platform.set_ad {"outcome":"closedEarly"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `outcome` | string ["watched","closedEarly","noFill","consentRefused"] | no | How the next ads end. |
| `gdpr` | string ["granted","denied","notRequired","unknown"] | no | What the GDPR (UMP) sheet answered. |
| `tracking` | string ["authorized","denied","notDetermined","restricted","notRequired"] | no | What the tracking (ATT) sheet answered. |
| `privacyOptions` | string ["required","notRequired","unknown"] | no | Whether the consent form for changing ad choices is required (ads.consent privacyOptions). |

### `platform.set_fake` (modifies state)

Since 0.2.0.

Change how the fake platform backend behaves: signed in or out, how many frames it holds its answers, and the time of its cloud saves.

`signedIn: false` makes every method but player.signIn answer notSignedIn (and sends a `player` event); `delayFrames: n` holds each answer for n engine frames (0, the default, answers at once), so a test can look at the "waiting" state of a screen and game.step() until the answer arrives. Give any of them. `cloudClock: n` sets the time (Unix seconds) the next cloud.save gets as its modified time, which cloud.stat reports; it starts at 1767225600 (2026-01-01T00:00:00Z) and goes up by one second with each save, so saves are ordered without the wall clock. `backend: "none"` makes the fake behave as the none backend (platform.has false for every service, every call rejects `unavailable`, signIn answers signed out) until platform.reset. Fails when the game runs a real store backend. Example: platform.set_fake {"delayFrames":2}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `signedIn` | boolean | no | false: the player is not signed in. |
| `backend` | string ["fake","none"] | no | "none": behave as the none backend until platform.reset. |
| `delayFrames` | integer | no | Frames each answer is held (0 = at once). |
| `cloudClock` | integer | no | Unix seconds the next cloud.save is stamped with (cloud.stat's modified). |

### `platform.state`

Since 0.2.0.

Show which platform backend runs, its services, the player, the declared ids and, for the fake backend, everything it holds.

Returns {backend, why, adsBackend, adsWhy, httpBackend, httpWhy, networkHosts, audience, underAge, services, player: {id, name, signedIn}, catalog: {achievements, stats, leaderboards, products, placements} (the ids factoria.json "platform" declares), pending (requests waiting for an answer), fake?} where `fake` (only when the backend is the fake) is {signedIn, delayFrames, frame, achievements: {id: {unlocked, progress}}, stats: {id: value}, leaderboards: {id: best} (a daily or weekly board: "id@periodKey"), cloud: {key: text}, cloudModified: {key: unix seconds}, cloudClock, remotePlay: [session], owned: [productId], unfinished: [{transactionId, productId, receipt}], presence: {text, data}, ads: {outcome, gdpr, tracking, shown, rewarded}, scripted: {method: answers queued}, held, calls: [{seq, frame, method, args, ok, result | error, scripted?}], callsDropped}. `calls` is every request the game made, with the arguments the backend got (store ids included) and how it was answered: assert on it after game.step. `adsBackend` is the backend that answers ads.* (an ads plugin such as admob, the store backend when it offers ads, or "none") and `adsWhy` says why; `audience` is factoria.json platform.ads.audience and `underAge` what platform.ads.setUnderAge answered (true for a children's game, null if not asked). `httpBackend` is what answers http.fetch (the system HTTP client such as curl or winhttp in a windowed run or a shipped game, the fake in tests and headless runs, or "none"), `httpWhy` says why (also why a client cannot run) and `networkHosts` is the hosts factoria.json "network" declares. Example: platform.state {}

## play

### `play.report`

What happened while the user played: perf, spikes, warnings/errors, their problem marks and screenshots.

Call it when the user says they played the game and saw problems (slow, ugly UI, bugs). Returns the session.json content (perf: avg/p95/max frame ms and frames over 16.7/33 ms; profile: where the time went, per engine system, per script behaviour class (ms and calls per frame, slowest first), GPU ms or null + reason, memory; spikes: slowest frames with entity count and render stats; logs: warnings and errors; marks: frame, time, note and screenshot path, 1-based `n`), `replay` (the input file, absolute path) and `replayHow`. The result carries ONE picture ($image): the screenshot of mark `mark` (default 1); call again with mark 2, 3... to see the others. `session` defaults to the latest (see play.sessions). Example: play.report {"mark":2}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `session` | string | no | Session folder name from play.sessions. Default: the latest. |
| `mark` | integer | no | Which mark's screenshot to attach as the picture. Default 1. |

### `play.sessions`

List the recent play sessions recorded by the editor (Play .. Stop), newest first.

Each session is a folder .factoria/sessions/<yyyymmdd-hhmmss>/ written when the user pressed Stop in the editor. Rows have a short summary: scene, duration, frame time p95/max, number of warnings/errors and the user's marks (notes). Call play.report {session} for the details and screenshots. Example: play.sessions {"max":5}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max` | integer | no | How many sessions to list. Default 10. |

## project

### `player.run_ios_sim` (modifies state)

Since 0.3.0.

Play an input replay on the iOS player in the iOS Simulator (an iPhone or an iPad), turn the screen and take a screenshot.

Needs a Mac with Xcode. `xcrun simctl` can neither tap nor rotate, so the player takes both itself: this command boots a simulator, installs `app` (the Simulator build of the player, ./build_ios.sh --simulator in the iOS export folder), launches it with the environment variables FA_INPUT_REPLAY (the replay `input.record` writes, the one `factoria run --input` plays) and FA_ORIENTATION (portrait or landscape; iOS refuses an orientation the Info.plist does not allow), waits for the player's "player: replay done after N frames" line (without `input`: for its 60-frame run marker), waits `settleMilliseconds` more, writes a PNG of the simulator's screen when `screenshot` is given and terminates the app. The replay is applied by frame number to the window's frames at their real duration (not the fixed step of a headless run): presses and releases play as recorded, but a game that moves by dt may end up elsewhere than in the recording, so check what it leaves with the screenshot and the `console`. Returns {device, deviceName, bundleId, replayFrames, finished, orientationRequested, screenshot, errors[], console[] (the last 80 lines), nextSteps[], ok}; it is an error (with the end of the console in its message) when the replay does not end in `seconds` or the player logged an error. dryRun returns the simctl commands and runs nothing (any host). Example: {"app":"build/export/my-game-ios/build/Debug-iphonesimulator/factoria_player.app","input":"replays/play.json","device":"iPad Pro 13-inch","orientation":"landscape","screenshot":"build/ipad.png"}.

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `app` | string | yes | The player built for the iOS Simulator: a factoria_player.app folder (project-relative or absolute). |
| `input` | string | no | An input replay JSON ({"frames":{"0":{"press":["jump"]}}}), project-relative, absolute or relative to the current folder. Without it the player just runs. |
| `orientation` | string ["portrait","landscape"] | no | Turn the screen to this orientation about a second after the start. |
| `device` | string | no | The simulator: a UDID or a name or part of one ("iPad Pro 13-inch"). Default: a booted iPhone, else the first iPhone of the newest iOS runtime. |
| `bundleId` | string | no | The app's bundle id. Default: read from the app's Info.plist. |
| `screenshot` | string | no | Write a PNG of the simulator's screen here when the replay is done (project-relative, inside the project, or absolute). |
| `seconds` | integer | no | How long to wait for the replay to finish. Default 90. |
| `settleMilliseconds` | integer | no | Wait this long after the last replay frame before the screenshot. Default 1500. |
| `dryRun` | boolean | no | Return the simctl commands and run nothing. Default false. |

## scene

### `prefab.save` (modifies state)

Save an entity of the running world, with its children, as a prefab file.

Writes {"format":"factoria.prefab/1","entity":{...}} in the canonical compact layout (the one scene.save and scene.format write), ready to commit and to instantiate with scene.spawn {"prefab":path}, a scene entity {"prefab":path} or a scene.import_ascii legend. `id` is the id (or name) of an entity of the running world; the whole tree below it is saved with every component's non-default serialized fields (runtime state such as velocities and animation time is not). A prefab describes the reusable thing, not this instance, so the file does NOT carry: the ids (every instantiation gets fresh ones; an id stays only where another entity of the saved tree points at it through an Entity field, so those references survive); the root's Transform.position (where the instance happens to stand: the spawn call, the scene entity or the legend places each new instance; children keep their positions relative to the root; rotation and scale are kept); tags starting with 'tilemap:' (scene.import_ascii adds them to the objects it places, and a prefab carrying one would be destroyed when that map is re-imported); Entity fields pointing at an entity outside the saved tree (they would dangle). An entity created from a prefab saves fully expanded (no `prefab` key). To keep the exact position, save the whole world with scene.save instead. `path` is project-relative (or absolute inside the project), must end in .prefab.json and normally lives in prefabs/. An existing file is NOT replaced unless `overwrite` is true. Returns {path, entity (id of the saved entity in the running world), children (number of saved descendants), overwritten, notes?}; `notes` lists what was left out of the file when something noteworthy was. Errors name the id with did-you-mean suggestions or the path rule with a corrected name. Example: prefab.save {"id":"enemy_3","path":"prefabs/enemy.prefab.json"}

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | yes | Id (or name) of the entity to save; its children are saved with it. |
| `path` | string | yes | Project-relative output path ending in .prefab.json, e.g. prefabs/enemy.prefab.json. |
| `overwrite` | boolean | no | Replace the file when it already exists. Without it an existing file is an error. Default false. |

## project

### `project.add_menu_kit` (modifies state)

Since 0.3.0.

Copy the menu kit (main menu, options, pause, loading screen, ...) into the game and merge its strings into the locales.

The menu kit of docs/MENUS.md (templates/menus/ in the FactorIA install): `parts` picks what to copy, the files go to the same paths in the game (scripts/, scenes/, prefabs/ui/, tests/recipe.test.js) and the kit's strings are merged into locales/<language>.json for every language of factoria.json "localization" (added when the game has none). Scenes and prefabs are written in the canonical layout of scene.format. Parts that others need come along (the main menu needs core, options and credits) and are listed in `requiredBy`. The shop, ageGate and analyticsConsent parts are optional for the main menu: its Shop button, shop panel, age gate call and analytics question call are written only when those parts are added (all parts by default). A kit file the game already has and has changed is NOT touched unless `overwrite` is true: it is listed in `skipped`; a file that is the same is listed in `unchanged`, so running the command twice changes nothing. String keys the game already has are never replaced, with or without `overwrite`; only missing ones are added. A language the kit has no texts for gets the English ones. The "pause" part also adds the input action "pause" to factoria.json when it is missing. Returns {parts[], requiredBy{}, added[], unchanged[], overwritten[], skipped[{file,reason}], locales[{file,created,merged[],skipped[]}], settings[], nextSteps[]}. Examples: {} (all parts), {"parts":["pause"]}, {"parts":["main-menu","loading"],"overwrite":true}.

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `parts` | array | no | Which parts to add; default all. Parts and what they copy: core: Shared by every menu: the player's settings saved in storage (scripts/settings.js), the stack of panels that open over each other (scripts/ui/menu_stack.js), read-aloud for focused widgets (scripts/ui/read_aloud.js) and the menu.* strings.; options: The options panel: video, a colour filter, audio per bus, controls (rebinding every action of the game) and language, saved between runs (prefabs/ui/options.prefab.json, scripts/ui/options.js). The textSpeed part adds a dialogue "Text speed" row to the audio tab; addOptionsRow() of scripts/ui/options.js adds a row of the game to any tab.; textSpeed: A "Text speed" row in the options panel's audio tab (slow, normal, fast, instant), saved as settings.textSpeed in characters per second; the game's dialogue box reveals a line with Text.visibleCharacters = revealedCharacters(seconds) (scripts/settings.js). Without this part the options prefab has no such row (all parts by default).; credits: The credits panel that lists the software inside the runtime (scripts/ui/credits.js).; shop: The shop panel for in-app purchases (scripts/ui/shop.js) and the behaviour that pauses a level while the store's overlay is open (scripts/store_events.js). Needs the products in factoria.json "platform" (docs/PLATFORM.md).; ageGate: The age gate for a game whose ads reach children and adults (factoria.json platform.ads.audience "mixed"): a neutral birth-year screen (prefabs/ui/age_gate.prefab.json, scripts/ui/age_gate.js) that tells the ad network whether the player is under the age of consent with platform.ads.setUnderAge(). The main menu, when added too, opens it once, before any ad; its tests/age_gate.test.js checks it.; analyticsConsent: The analytics question for a game whose factoria.json has an "analytics" section (docs/ANALYTICS.md): a short screen (prefabs/ui/analytics_consent.prefab.json, scripts/ui/analytics_consent.js) that asks once whether the game may count anonymous usage, and gives the answer to analytics.setConsent(). Nothing is sent before it. The main menu, when added too, opens it on its first run; the Options switch (options part) changes the answer later. tests/analytics_consent.test.js checks it.; main-menu: The title screen: scenes/menu.scene.json (Play, Options, Credits, Quit, with the options and credits panels in it), scripts/main_menu.js, and tests/recipe.test.js, the kit's test, which drives the menu with a gamepad only. Needs core, options and credits. The Shop button and panel, the line that opens the age gate and the line that opens the analytics question are written only when the shop, ageGate and analyticsConsent parts are added too (all parts by default).; pause: The pause menu (prefabs/ui/pause.prefab.json, scripts/pause_menu.js): Resume, Options, Main menu. Put one entity with scripts/pause_menu.js in every level; adds the "pause" action to factoria.json when the game has none.; loading: The loading screen (scenes/loading.scene.json, scripts/loading.js): the main menu's Play button goes through it to the first level.; keyboard: The on-screen keyboard for a player without a physical one (prefabs/ui/keyboard.prefab.json, scripts/ui/keyboard.js): put one entity with the script in every scene that has a TextField.; slots: Save slots (scripts/slots.js, scripts/ui/slot_screen.js, prefabs/ui/slots.prefab.json, prefabs/ui/slot_dialog.prefab.json, tests/slots.test.js): five named slots and an autosave in storage, each a record with a counter, name, chapter, play time, picture and the game's data, the cloud merge by counter, and the save / load screen with a dialog that names a save (the on-screen keyboard opens for a gamepad player). Needs core and keyboard. The game supplies what is saved and how a slot is loaded: docs/MENUS.md, "Save slots".; dialogue: Subtitles for spoken lines and hints: say(key, {sound, speaker}) in scripts/dialogue.js, drawn by a Captions entity. Its strings are the example lines captions.* (replace them with the game's own).; card: A choice card for events, stories and decisions (scripts/ui/card.js, prefabs/ui/card.prefab.json): a modal panel (Panel.modal) with a title, a wrapped body, choice buttons that each have a detail line, a choice greyed out with its reason, a result stage with Continue, and an option to hold the game clock (game.paused) while it is open. The mouse, the arrows and the pad reach only the card. tests/card.test.js checks it.; cameraRig: The strategy camera for a management or strategy game (scripts/camera_rig.js): put the script on the orthographic camera. Drag pan, keys, screen-edge pan, wheel zoom towards the cursor between zoomMin and zoomMax, and a limit from the bounds() of an entity; it ignores the wheel and drags over the UI. Adds the input actions camera_drag, camera_left, camera_right, camera_up, camera_down, camera_zoom_in and camera_zoom_out to factoria.json when the game has none of that name. tests/camera_rig.test.js checks it. |
| `overwrite` | boolean | no | Replace a kit file the game has changed (a file that is the same is left alone). Without it that file is left as it is and listed in `skipped`. String keys the game has are never replaced. Default false. |

### `project.create` (modifies state)

Create a new game project from a template.

Creates `dir` (relative to the server's working directory unless absolute) with factoria.json, a scene, scripts, a test, AGENTS.md, ENGINE_FEEDBACK.json and the real types/factoria.d.ts. Afterwards start `factoria mcp --project <dir>` to work on it. Example: {"dir":"my-game","template":"2d-platformer","name":"My Game"}.

| Argument | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dir` | string | yes | Target folder (created; must be empty or new). |
| `template` | string | no | 2d-empty, 2d-platformer or 3d-empty (see project.templates). Default "2d-empty". |
| `name` | string | no | Display name (default: folder name). |
| `id` | string | no | Reverse-DNS id, e.g. com.example.mygame. |

### `project.export` (modifies state)

Since 0.1.2.

Package the game for a platform: a desktop bundle, an Android APK/AAB, an iOS project, or a web page (HTML5).
